issues: 賢明肩比 ("the wise stand shoulder to shoulder", i.e. are many) read as "the wise and brilliant were comparable".
en_revised: Fourteen or fifteen *li* to the southwest of the great city, one reaches the old city of Śākala (奢羯羅故城). Although the walls are ruined, the foundations remain solid. It is over twenty *li* in circumference. Within it, a smaller city has been built, six or seven *li* in circumference, where the inhabitants are wealthy; this is the former capital of this country. Several hundred years ago, there was a king named Mihirakula (摩醯邏矩羅) (translated as "Great Clan" in Chinese), who made this city his capital and ruled over all of India. He possessed talent and wisdom, and his nature was brave and fierce; there was no neighboring country that did not submit to him. During his leisure from state affairs, he wished to study the Buddha-dharma and ordered the monks to recommend a person of outstanding virtue. At that time, the monks dared not respond to the order, for they were few in desire and practiced non-action, not seeking fame or status; those who were learned and brilliant feared his majesty. At that time, there was a former servant of the royal household who had long worn the dyed robes (i.e., was a monk), whose rhetoric was refined and elegant, and whose speech was eloquent and quick; the assembly collectively recommended him to respond to the order. The King said, "I respect the Buddha-dharma and have sought out famous monks from afar, yet the assembly recommends this menial to engage in discussion with me. I always thought that among the monks the wise and brilliant stood shoulder to shoulder; now that I know this, what is there to respect?" Thereupon, he issued a decree throughout the five regions of India that from then on, the Buddha-dharma was to be utterly destroyed, and all monks were to be expelled until not a single one remained. King Bālāditya (婆羅阿迭多) (translated as "Young Sun" in Chinese) of the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) revered the Buddha-dharma and loved his people; because of King Mihirakula’s excessive punishments and tyrannical rule, he guarded his own borders and did not offer the customary tribute. At that time, King Mihirakula mobilized his troops, intending to punish him. When King Bālāditya (幼日王) learned of this news, he told his ministers, "I hear the invaders are coming, but I cannot bear to let my soldiers engage in battle. I hope my officials and the common people will forgive me for this, and I shall take this humble body and hide in the marshes and wilderness." Having finished speaking, he left the palace and took refuge in the mountains and forests. Several tens of thousands of people in the country, moved by gratitude and admiration, followed him and hid on islands in the sea. King Mihirakula (大族王) entrusted his troops to his younger brother and sailed across the sea to attack him. King Bālāditya guarded the strategic passes and sent light cavalry to lure the enemy into battle; at the first sound of the gongs and drums, ambushers rose from all sides, capturing Mihirakula alive and leading him forward with his hands tied behind his back. King Mihirakula, ashamed of his failure, covered his face with his garment. King Bālāditya sat upon his lion throne, surrounded by his officials, and ordered his attendants to say to Mihirakula, "Uncover your face, for I have words for you." Mihirakula replied, "The positions of subject and master have been reversed, and we look upon each other as enemies; since we are not on friendly terms, what is the use of speaking face to face?" Though they urged him again and again, he would not comply. Thereupon, the King issued a proclamation enumerating his crimes, saying, "The Three Jewels are a field of merit upon which the four forms of birth depend. You have acted like a jackal or wolf, destroying these noble works. Fortune has not protected you, and you have been captured by me. Your crimes are unpardonable, and you must face the penalty of the law." At that time, the mother of King Bālāditya was widely learned and possessed a keen memory, and she was highly skilled in physiognomy. Hearing that he was about to execute Mihirakula, she hurriedly told King Bālāditya, "I have heard that Mihirakula possesses an extraordinary appearance and great wisdom; I wish to see him once." King Bālāditya ordered that Mihirakula be led into his mother's palace. The mother of Bālāditya (幼日王) said, "Alas, Mihirakula (大族), I pray you do not feel ashamed! The world is impermanent, and honor and disgrace alternate. I am like a mother to you, and you are like a son to me; you should remove the cloth covering your face and speak to me face to face."  Mihirakula said, "Formerly the ruler of a hostile state, I am now a captive prisoner. Having ruined the royal enterprise and extinguished the ancestral sacrifices, I am ashamed before the spirits of my ancestors above and the common people below; I am truly disgraced to show my face. Looking up and down between heaven and earth, I cannot bear the loss of myself, and that is why I cover my face."  The king's mother said, "Rise and fall follow the times; existence and extinction have their destiny. If you use the mind to equalize things, then gain and loss are both forgotten; if you use things to equalize the mind, then praise and blame arise in turn. You should believe in karmic retribution and move along with the times. Remove your covering and speak; perhaps you may preserve your life."  Mihirakula thanked her, saying, "Being a man of no talent, I inherited the royal throne, yet my governance strayed from the Way, leading to the ruin of my kingdom. Although I am now in bonds, I still cling to the hope of living for a little longer. I dare to accept your great kindness and will uncover my face to thank you for your profound grace."  Thereupon, he removed the cloth and revealed his face. The king's mother said, "Take care of yourself, for you shall live out your natural lifespan."  Soon after, she told King Bālāditya, "The ancient scriptures contain the teaching to forgive transgressions and cherish life. Although King Mihirakula has accumulated evil for a long time, his remaining merit is not yet exhausted. If you kill this man, for twelve years there will be famine and suffering. However, he possesses the energy of a restoration; he will not ultimately be a king of a great country, but he shall occupy the north and possess a small territory." King Bālāditya, obeying his compassionate mother's command and pitying the sovereign who had lost his kingdom, gave him a young daughter in marriage and treated him with extraordinary courtesy; he assembled the king's remaining troops and provided additional guards before they had even left the island. The younger brother of King Mihirakula returned to his country and established himself as ruler; having lost his throne, Mihirakula fled to hide in the mountains and wilderness, eventually seeking refuge in the north in the kingdom of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國). The King of Kaśmīra treated him with great courtesy and, pitying him for the loss of his kingdom, granted him a territory as a fief. After some time had passed, he led his townspeople, treacherously killed the King of Kaśmīra, and established himself as ruler. Taking advantage of the prestige of his victory, he attacked the kingdom of Gandhāra (健馱邏國) to the west; by deploying hidden troops and an ambush, he killed its king and completely exterminated the royal clan and the high ministers. He destroyed one thousand six hundred stūpas and sanghārāmas. Beyond those killed in battle, there were nine hundred million people whom he intended to execute, leaving no survivors. At that time, his assistants all remonstrated, saying, "The Great King has intimidated powerful enemies and, without engaging in battle, has executed the chief culprits. What fault have the common people committed? We wish to offer our own humble bodies to die in their stead." The King replied, "You believe in the Buddha-dharma, value merit in the afterlife, aspire to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, and speak extensively on the Jātakas; do you wish to transmit my evil deeds to future generations? You should return to your positions and speak no more of this." Thereupon, he took three hundred million of the upper-class families and had them killed at the bank of the Sindhu (信度) River; three hundred million of the middle-class families were drowned and killed in the Sindhu River; and three hundred million of the lower-class families were distributed among the soldiers. Having seized the wealth of the ruined state, he gathered his troops and returned. Before a year had passed, he suddenly died. At that time, clouds and fog grew dark and gloomy, the great earth shook, and violent winds raged. A person who had attained the fruit (of the path) felt pity and sighed, saying, "By unjustly killing the innocent and destroying the Buddha-dharma, he has fallen into the Avīci hell, to transmigrate without end."  In the old city of Śākala (奢羯羅故城), there is a monastery (saṃghārāma) with more than one hundred monks, all of whom study the Hīnayāna teachings. The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親) formerly composed the *Paramārthasaptati* (勝義諦論) here. Beside it is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, where the four past Buddhas preached the Dharma. There is also a site with traces of the four Buddhas walking in meditation. Five or six li to the northwest of the monastery is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which is the place where the four past Buddhas preached the Dharma. More than ten li to the northeast of the new capital city, one reaches a stone stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka, which is the place where the Tathāgata halted midway while traveling north to spread his teachings. The *Account of India* (印度記) says, "There are many relics within the stūpa, and on days of fasting, it sometimes emits light."
li_quote: I thought that there were many brilliant scholars in the community of monks

issues: 此國則冬所居也 is the hostages' winter residence (質子…三時易館), not Kaniṣka's; "his" points to the king.
en_revised: Traveling eastward from here for more than five hundred li, one arrives at the country of Cīnabhukti (至那僕底國) (within the borders of North India). The country of Cīnabhukti is more than two thousand li in circuit. The capital city is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit. The crops are lush and abundant, but fruit trees are sparse. The households are settled in their occupations, and the national resources are plentiful. The climate is warm and hot; the customs of the people are timid and weak. Their studies encompass both the true and the conventional, and their faith includes both the heterodox and the orthodox. There are ten saṃghārāmas and eight deva temples.  In the past, during the reign of King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王), his reputation shook neighboring countries and his might extended to distant lands; the border tribes west of the river feared his power and sent hostages. Once King Kaniṣka had obtained the hostages, he treated them with great generosity and favor, changing their residences according to the three seasons and providing guards from the four branches of the military. This country was the hostages' winter residence, and therefore it is called Cīnabhukti (which in the language of the Tang means "Han Fief"). Because it was the place where the hostages resided, it became the name of the country.  From this region onward, as far as the various parts of India, the land had no pears or peaches. They were planted by the hostages, and thus peaches are called *cīnānī* (至那爾) (which in the language of the Tang means "brought from Han"), and pears are called *cīnarājaputra* (至那羅闍弗呾邏) (which in the language of the Tang means "Han Prince"). Therefore, the people of this country deeply revere the eastern lands, and they point to one another and say, "These are the people from the original country of our former king."
li_quote: The winter residence of the hostage was in this district

issues: 賢劫千佛皆於此地集天、人眾: the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa are mostly still to come; past tense "all gathered" is wrong (Li: "will hold").
en_revised: Traveling more than five hundred *li* to the southeast of the great city, one arrives at the Tamasavana Monastery (答秣蘇伐那僧伽藍) (in the Tang language, "Dark Forest"). There are more than three hundred monks who study the Sarvāstivāda school; their deportment is solemn and their moral conduct is lofty, and they are particularly well-versed in the studies of the Lesser Vehicle. The thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa all gather assemblies of gods and humans in this place to preach the profound and wonderful Dharma. In the three-hundredth year after the Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the master Kātyāyana (formerly called Jiazhanyan [迦旃延], which is erroneous) composed the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* here. Within the Tamasavana Monastery, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. Small stūpas and various large stone chambers stand facing one another like the scales of a fish, in numbers too many to detail; these are all places where the various sages who have attained fruition since the beginning of the *kalpa* have entered into extinction, and it is difficult to enumerate them all, though their teeth and bones still remain. The monasteries surrounding the mountain cover a circuit of twenty *li*, and there are hundreds of thousands of stūpas containing the Buddha’s relics, with their corners connected and their shadows touching.
li_quote: All the thousand buddhas of the bhadrakalpa will hold meetings of heavenly and human beings at this place

issues: 氣序逾寒 is "colder", not "extremely cold" (it goes with 霜雪微降); 遺迹斯記 means the stūpa marks the traces of his visit, not "this record remains of his traces".
en_revised: From here, traveling northeast, crossing steep ridges, traversing deep valleys, passing over perilous routes, and wading through dangerous paths for more than seven hundred *li*, one reaches the country of Kulūta (屈露多國) (屈 is read 居勿反) (within the borders of North India). The country of Kulūta is more than three thousand *li* in circuit, with mountains surrounding its four borders. The capital city of the country is fourteen or fifteen *li* in circuit. The land is fertile, grain is sown in its season, flowers and fruits are abundant, and plants and trees flourish. As it borders the Snow Mountains (Himālaya), it is rich in precious medicinal herbs and produces gold, silver, red copper, as well as fire-pearls and rain-stones. The climate is colder, and frost and snow fall lightly. The people are coarse and ugly in appearance, and are prone to goiters and swollen feet; their nature is fierce and impetuous, and they value spirit and courage. There are more than twenty *saṃghārāmas* (伽藍) with over one thousand monks, most of whom study the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), while few practice the various schools (Hīnayāna). There are fifteen *deva* temples, where followers of different paths live together. Relying on cliffs and occupying ridges, stone chambers are situated at intervals, some being dwellings of *arhats* and others being places where *ṛṣis* (仙人) have stayed. In the country there is a *stūpa* built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata came to this country, preached the Dharma to save people, and the stūpa marks his traces.
li_quote: In this country there is a stupa built by King Aśoka in memory of the event of the Tathāgata coming to this place in olden times

issues: 曼殊室利…諸菩薩窣堵波等: Mañjuśrī heads the stūpas of Bodhisattvas, not the list of holy disciples (釋迦如來諸聖弟子 ends with 羅怙羅).
en_revised: From here, traveling east more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Mathurā (秣菟羅國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Mathurā is more than five thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty *li* in circuit. The land is fertile and rich, and the people are devoted to agriculture. Every household plants mango trees to form groves; although they share the same name, there are two varieties: the small ones are green when raw and yellow when ripe, while the large ones remain green from beginning to end. The country produces fine striped cotton cloth and gold. The climate is hot, and the customs are honest and compliant; the people delight in cultivating merit for the afterlife, and they revere virtue and value learning. There are more than twenty monasteries and over two thousand monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles with equal diligence. There are five *deva* temples, where followers of various heterodox sects live together. There are three *stūpas* that were all built by King Aśoka. There are many traces of the four past Buddhas. There are *stūpas* containing the relics of the holy disciples of the Śākya Tathāgata, namely: Śāriputra (formerly called Shelizi or Shelifu, which are erroneous abbreviations), Maudgalyāyana (formerly called Mujianlian, which is erroneous), Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra (called Manci Zi in the Tang language; formerly called Miduoluonizi, which is an erroneous abbreviation), Upāli, Ānanda, Rāhula (formerly called Luohou or Luoyun, both of which are erroneous abbreviations); and *stūpas* of Bodhisattvas such as Mañjuśrī (called Miaojixiang [妙吉祥] in the Tang language; formerly called Rushou [濡首], also Wenshushili [文殊師利], or sometimes Manshushili [曼殊尸利], translated as 'Wonderful Virtue' [妙德], which is erroneous), and others. During the three long fast months of every year and the six fast days of every month, the members of the Saṅgha compete with one another, leading those of like mind to bring offerings and prepare many rare curiosities, presenting them before the images of their respective patrons. Those who study the Abhidharma make offerings to Śāriputra; those who practice meditation make offerings to Maudgalyāyana; those who recite and uphold the Sūtras make offerings to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra; those who study the Vinaya make offerings to Upāli; the various bhikṣuṇīs make offerings to Ānanda; those who have not yet received the full ordination make offerings to Rāhula; and those who study the Mahāyāna make offerings to the various Bodhisattvas. On these days, the various stūpas compete in performing offerings; pearl-adorned banners are arrayed in rows, precious canopies are lined up, smoke from incense is like clouds, and flowers are scattered like rain, obscuring the sun and moon and shaking the valleys. The king and his ministers make the cultivation of merit their primary duty.
li_quote: There are stupas for such bodhisattvas as Mañjuśrī

issues: 王以為 is one king (the next sentence has the king alone commissioning the book), not "the kings"; 權可立功 is "a stratagem can achieve success", not "authority can establish merit".
en_revised: Within a radius of two hundred li around the great city, the people of that land call it the Land of Blessedness (Kurukṣetra). According to the records of former times, the Five Indias were once ruled by two kings; their territories bordered each other and were subject to mutual invasions, with wars never ceasing. The two rulers conspired together, wishing to decide the matter through a decisive battle to determine the victor and bring peace to the populace. The common people were all resentful and would not follow the kings' commands. The king thought that it is difficult to plan the beginning of an undertaking with the masses, but that the divine can move living beings and a stratagem can achieve success. At that time, there was a Brahman known for his great talent; the king secretly presented him with a gift of silk and ordered him into the rear palace to compose a sacred text, which was then hidden in a mountain cave. As time passed, the trees grew to the size of a man’s embrace. The king sat in court and told his ministers: "Because of my lack of virtue, I unworthily occupy this high position; yet the Emperor of Heaven has looked down upon me and granted me a spiritual book in a dream, which is now located on a certain mountain, hidden on a certain ridge." Thereupon, he issued an order to search for it, and the book was found beneath the mountain forest. The officials offered congratulations, and the masses were joyful; it was proclaimed far and near, so that all might hear and know of it. Its general purport was: "Life and death are without bounds, and the cycle of transmigration is endless; sentient beings are submerged and drowning, with no way to save themselves. I, through a marvelous stratagem, shall cause them to depart from all suffering. Now, this royal city and its surroundings of two hundred li were a land of blessings and merit in the ages of former emperors. As the years and months have been extremely long, the inscriptions and records have been obliterated; living beings do not realize this and have consequently sunk into the sea of suffering. If they are drowning and not saved, what is to be said of it?" "All you sentient beings, if you die facing the enemy in battle, you will be reborn among humans; if you slaughter many of the innocent, you will receive the blessings and joys of heaven; and if obedient grandsons and filial sons who serve their elderly parents travel through this land, they shall obtain infinite blessings. With so little effort yielding such great merit, how could you let this advantage slip away? Once you lose this human body, the three paths (the three lower realms of existence) are dark and obscure. Therefore, let all living beings each apply themselves to their practice!" Thereupon, the people all engaged in battle, viewing death as a return home. The king then issued an order to recruit the brave and fierce; the two kingdoms joined in battle, and the piled-up corpses were like dense grass. Down to the present day, skeletal remains are scattered across the fields; as the events took place in ancient times, the human bones are of a massive size. Local custom passes down the name of this place as the Land of Blessings (Kurukṣetra). Four or five li to the northwest of the city, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). The bricks are all a yellowish-red color and are very bright and clean. Inside is one *dou* of the Tathāgata’s relics, which emit light from time to time and manifest many divine wonders.
li_quote: the king [of Sthāneśvara] considered that the gods might be able to arouse his people and their power might help him achieve his exploits

issues: 舍利子、沒特伽羅諸阿羅漢: Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana "and other arhats"; the en limits the dozens of stūpas to the two.
en_revised: From here, traveling northeast for more than four hundred li, one arrives at the country of Srughna (窣祿勤那國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Srughna is over six thousand li in circuit; it borders the Ganges (gaṅgā) river to the east, rests against great mountains to the north, and the Yamunā river flows through the middle of its territory. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circuit; it borders the Yamunā river to the east. Although it is very desolate, its foundations remain firm. The produce of the land and the suitability of the climate are the same as in the country of Sthāneśvara (薩他泥濕伐羅國). The people are honest and simple by nature, and they revere and believe in non-Buddhist paths. They value the arts and sciences, and esteem both merit and wisdom. There are five monasteries with over one thousand monks, most of whom study the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), while few study other schools. They deliberate on subtle doctrines and engage in pure, profound discussions; talented scholars from distant regions come here to investigate doctrines and resolve doubts. There are one hundred Deva temples, and the non-Buddhist sects are very numerous. To the southeast of the great city, on the west bank of the Yamunā river and outside the eastern gate of a large monastery, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata once preached the Dharma here to save people. Beside it is another stūpa, which contains the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. Surrounding it on the left and right are several dozen stūpas containing the hair and nails of Śāriputra (舍利子), Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅), and other arhats. After the Tathāgata entered extinction, this country was misled by various non-Buddhists; they accepted and followed erroneous teachings and abandoned correct views. The five monasteries that exist today were built at the sites where masters from other countries held debates and emerged victorious over various non-Buddhists and Brahmins.
li_quote: Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and other arhats are preserved in several tens of stupas

issues: 我今欲破眾賢之論，若指諸掌 is hypothetical ("were I to refute it, it would be as easy…"), not a declared intention, which contradicts what follows (he preserves the work); 駁斥先進 is "refuted my predecessor" (Vasubandhu), not "advanced teachings".
en_revised: Crossing the river to the east bank, one arrives at the country of Matipura (秣底補羅國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Matipura is over six thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circuit. It is suitable for grain and wheat, and there are many flowers and fruits. The climate is harmonious and pleasant, and the customs are simple and honest. The people esteem learning and the arts, and are deeply skilled in magical incantations. Those who believe in heterodox paths and those who believe in the orthodox path are about equal in number. The king is of the Śūdra caste; he does not believe in the Buddha-Dharma and reverently serves the heavenly deities. There are more than ten monasteries with over eight hundred monks, most of whom study the Sarvāstivāda school of the Lesser Vehicle teachings. There are more than fifty temples to the heavenly deities, where followers of different paths live together. Four or five li to the south of the great city, one reaches a small monastery with over fifty monks. In the past, the master of treatises Guṇaprabha (in the Tang language, "Virtue-Light") composed the *Tattvavibhaṅga* (辯真) and other treatises here, totaling over one hundred works. The master of treatises was heroic and outstanding in his youth, and broad-minded and quick-witted in his maturity; he was widely learned and possessed a retentive memory, being a scholar of great erudition. Originally, he studied the Mahayana, but not having exhausted its profound mysteries, he read the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* and subsequently abandoned his former studies to learn the Lesser Vehicle. He composed several dozen treatises, refuting the principles of the Mahayana and establishing the attachments of the Lesser Vehicle. He also produced several dozen secular books, criticizing and rejecting the canonical treatises composed by his predecessors. He pondered the Buddhist scriptures deeply, but there were over ten points he could not resolve; though he studied them with refinement for a long time, his doubts remained. At that time, there was an arhat named Devasena (in the Tang language, "Heavenly Army") who traveled back and forth to the Tuṣita Heaven. Guṇaprabha wished to see Maitreya to resolve his doubts and request further instruction. Devasena, using his supernatural powers, took him up to the heavenly palace. Upon seeing Maitreya (慈氏 - *Maitreya*), he merely made a long bow and did not prostrate. Devasena said to him, "Maitreya Bodhisattva is the next to succeed to the Buddha’s throne; why are you so arrogant that you dare not show him respect? You are seeking to receive instruction, so how can you not humble yourself?" Guṇaprabha (德光 - *Guṇaprabha*) replied, "Venerable one, your words are indeed a guide. However, I am a fully ordained bhikṣu and a monastic disciple, while Maitreya Bodhisattva enjoys the bliss of heavenly rewards and is not a member of the monastic order; I fear it would be inappropriate for me to pay him homage." The Bodhisattva, knowing that his pride was deeply rooted and that he was not a vessel fit to hear the Dharma, allowed him to travel back and forth three times without resolving his doubts. Guṇaprabha asked Devasena again, wishing to pay homage once more, but Devasena, disgusted by his pride, ignored him and did not reply. Since Guṇaprabha did not have his wish fulfilled, he harbored resentment and went into the mountain forests to practice meditation for the attainment of supernatural powers; however, because his pride was not eliminated, he did not realize the fruits of the Path.  Three or four *li* to the north of the Guṇaprabha monastery, there is a large monastery with over two hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). This is the place where the master of treatises Saṃghabhadra (眾賢 - *Saṃghabhadra*) passed away. The master of treatises was a man from the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國 - *Kaśmīra*); he was intelligent and erudite, and from his youth he was renowned for his elegance, having studied the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (說一切有部毘婆沙論) with particular depth. At that time, there was the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親 - *Vasubandhu*), who was single-mindedly devoted to the profound Path and sought to understand the meaning beyond the words. He refuted the positions held by the masters of the *Vibhāṣā* and composed the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (阿毘達磨俱舍論), in which the language and meaning were skillful and the principles were lofty and refined. Saṃghabhadra (眾賢) read it and was moved to action. Thereupon, he delved deeply into study and research for twelve years, composing the *Hailstone on the Kośa* (俱舍雹論) in twenty-five thousand verses, totaling eight hundred thousand words. It was said that his words were profound and his reach far, exhausting the hidden and penetrating the subtle. He told his disciples, "With my outstanding talent and upholding my correct arguments, I shall drive back Vasubandhu (世親) and blunt his sharp edge, so that the old man may no longer enjoy a monopoly on pre-eminent fame." Thereupon, three or four of his most talented disciples took the treatise he had written and went to seek out Vasubandhu. At that time, Vasubandhu was in the city of Sākala (奢羯羅城) in the country of Takka (磔迦國). Word was sent from afar that Saṃghabhadra was arriving. Upon hearing this, Vasubandhu immediately began to pack his belongings. His disciples, filled with doubt, came forward to remonstrate, saying, "Great Master, your virtue surpasses that of former sages and your fame is unrivaled in the present age; among students near and far, there are none who do not defer to you. Now, hearing of Saṃghabhadra, why are you so flustered? If you must yield to him, we will be deeply ashamed." Vasubandhu replied, "I am traveling far away now, not to avoid this man. It is just that in this country, there are no longer any discerning scholars. Saṃghabhadra is a younger scholar whose sophistry flows like a river; I am old and frail and cannot engage in debate. I wish to defeat his heterodox views with a single word and lead him to Central India to face the eminent and learned scholars, so that they may discern truth from falsehood and examine right and wrong." He immediately ordered his companions to pack their book-satchels and set out on the long journey. The Master of Treatises Saṃghabhadra (眾賢) arrived at this monastery one day later, when he suddenly felt his vitality failing. He then composed a letter to apologize to Vasubandhu (世親), saying: "Since the Thus-Come One passed into extinction, the disciples have held to their own sectarian views, each transmitting their own school's learning, each specializing in their own field, favoring those who share their path and disparaging those of different schools. In my ignorance and dullness, I rashly received these traditions. Upon reading the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (阿毘達磨俱舍論) that you composed, which refutes the great principles of the Vaibhāṣika masters, I—without measuring my own strength—spent years in deep study and composed this treatise to uphold the orthodox school. My wisdom was small but my ambition was great, and now death is approaching. You, Bodhisattva, expound the subtle words and propagate the supreme truth; if you do not disparage my convictions and allow my writings to be preserved, I shall be fortunate indeed, and what regret could I have in death?" He then selected from among his disciples those who were eloquent and told them: "I am truly a junior scholar who has rashly insulted a senior master; such is my fate, what can be done? I am about to pass away. You must take this letter and the treatise I have composed, apologize to that Bodhisattva, and repent on my behalf." No sooner had he finished dictating these words than he suddenly passed away. The disciples took the letter to Vasubandhu and delivered the message, saying: "Our master Saṃghabhadra has already abandoned his life. He left a final letter to reproach himself and apologize for his faults. That his name not be forgotten is not something we would dare to hope for." Bodhisattva Vasubandhu read the letter and examined the treatise, and after pondering for a long time, he said to the disciples: "The Master of Treatises Saṃghabhadra was a clever junior; although his reasoning was insufficient, his rhetoric was more than enough. Were I now to refute Saṃghabhadra’s treatise, it would be as easy as pointing to the palm of my hand." "However, considering his dying request and valuing his challenging words, if it serves the great principles, I shall preserve his original intention; furthermore, this treatise clarifies my own school." He then changed the title to the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise Following the Correct Principles). His disciples remonstrated, saying: "While Saṃghabhadra was still alive, the Master withdrew far away; now that you have obtained his treatise, you even change its title for him—how can all the students face the shame of this?" Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, wishing to remove their doubts, spoke a verse: "Like a lion king, avoiding a boar and going far away, the wise should know the victory or defeat of the two powers." After Saṃghabhadra died, they cremated his body and collected his bones. In the Āmra (mango) grove, two hundred paces northwest of the monastery, they erected a stūpa, which still exists today. Beside the Āmra grove is a stūpa containing the remains of the master Vimalamitra (in Tang language, "Stainless Friend"). The master was a man of the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國) and had renounced the household life in the Sarvāstivāda school. He extensively studied the various scriptures and researched heterodox treatises. He traveled through the five Indias, studied the profound texts of the Tripiṭaka, and having established his reputation and completed his work, he was about to return to his home country. Passing by the stūpa of the master Saṃghabhadra, he patted it and sighed, saying: "The master possessed such noble magnanimity and refined character, expounding the great principles; just as he was about to defeat the heterodox sects and establish the legacy of his own school, how is it that his years were not prolonged! I, Vimalamitra, humbly follow in his footsteps; I have long admired his righteousness and have cherished his virtue across the ages." "Although Vasubandhu (世親) has passed away, his school's teachings are still transmitted. I shall exhaust all my knowledge to compose various treatises, causing the scholars of Jambudvīpa (贍部洲) to abandon the name of the Mahāyāna and to efface the fame of Vasubandhu; this shall be my immortal achievement, fulfilling my long-held ambition." Having spoken these words, his mind became deranged, five tongues emerged from his mouth, and hot blood gushed forth. Knowing that his life was surely coming to an end, he composed a letter of repentance, saying: "The Mahāyāna teachings are the ultimate discourse within the Buddha-dharma. Their names and meanings are profound and absolute, and their principles are subtle and mysterious. Because of my ignorance, I lightly refuted my predecessor; the karmic retribution is clear, and it is fitting that my body should be destroyed. I dare to warn all students: take this as a lesson, guard your intentions, and do not harbor doubts." The great earth shook, and his life then ended. At the place where he died, the ground sank into a pit. His traveling companions cremated his corpse, collected the remains, and built a memorial over them. At that time, an Arhat (羅漢) saw this and sighed, saying: "Alas! How painful! This master of treatises, following his own emotions and holding to his views, slandered and disparaged the Mahāyāna, and has fallen into the Avīci (無間) hell."
li_quote: If I wish to confute this treatise it would be as easy as pointing at my palm.

issues: 更請天軍，重欲覲禮: Guṇaprabha asked Devasena because he himself wished to pay homage again; "requested Devasena to go and pay respects" makes Devasena the one paying respects.
en_revised: Four or five li south of the great city, one arrives at a small monastery with over fifty monks. In the past, the master of treatises Guṇaprabha (known in Chinese as De Guang, "Virtue-Light") composed the *Bian zhen lun* (Treatise on Distinguishing the Truth) and other works here, over a hundred works in all. As a youth, the master was heroic and outstanding; as he grew older, he became broad-minded and quick-witted, possessing vast knowledge and a retentive memory, and was a scholar of great learning. He originally studied the Mahāyāna, but not having exhausted its profound mysteries, he read the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* and subsequently abandoned his former studies to learn the Hīnayāna. He composed several dozen treatises to refute the principles of the Mahāyāna and establish Hīnayāna doctrines. He also authored several dozen secular works, criticizing and rejecting the treatises composed by his predecessors. He pondered the Buddhist scriptures deeply, yet there were over ten points he could not resolve; though he studied them with great refinement for a long time, his doubts remained. At that time, there was an arhat named Devasena (known in Chinese as Tian Jun, "Heavenly Army") who traveled to and from the Tuṣita Heaven. Guṇaprabha wished to see Maitreya to resolve his doubts and seek instruction. Devasena used his supernatural powers to take him up to the heavenly palace. Upon seeing Maitreya, he merely made a long bow and did not prostrate. Devasena said to him, "Maitreya Bodhisattva is the next to succeed to the Buddha's throne; why are you so arrogant that you dare not show him respect? You are about to receive instruction, so why do you not bow down?" Guṇaprabha replied, "Venerable one, your words are indeed a guide. However, I am a fully ordained bhikṣu and a monastic disciple, while the Bodhisattva Maitreya enjoys the bliss of heavenly rewards and is not a member of the monastic order; I fear it would be inappropriate for me to pay him homage." The Bodhisattva knew that his heart was firmly set on pride and that he was not a vessel capable of hearing the Dharma; Guṇaprabha went back and forth three times, yet could not resolve his doubts. He again asked Devasena (天軍), wishing to pay homage once more, but Devasena, loathing his arrogance, treated him with contempt and did not respond. Since Guṇaprabha (德光) did not have his wishes fulfilled, he gave rise to resentment and immediately went to the mountain forests to practice and develop supernatural powers and meditative concentration; however, because his pride was not yet eliminated, he did not realize the fruits of the Path.
li_quote: said to Devasena that he wished to see [Maitreya] Bodhisattva once more so as to worship him

issues: 世以女稱國 means a woman has reigned over the country for generations (hence 東女國, and 夫亦為王，不知政事 follows), not "the country has been named after women".
en_revised: In the Great Snow Mountains to the north of this country lies the kingdom of Suvarṇagotra (translated into Chinese as the "Gold Clan"). It produces superior gold, and is named accordingly. It is long from east to west and narrow from north to south; this is the Eastern Women's Kingdom. For generations a woman has reigned over the country. The husband is also called king, but he does not manage state affairs; the men's only duties are warfare and farming. The soil is suitable for winter wheat, and there is an abundance of sheep and horses. The climate is cold and harsh, and the people are impetuous and violent. To the east it borders the kingdom of Tubo, to the north it borders the kingdom of Khotan, and to the west it borders the kingdom of Sampaha.
li_quote: as it is has been ruled from generation to generation by a woman

issues: 大城側故伽藍中，有窣堵波: the stūpa is in the old monastery beside the city, not "beside the old saṃghārāma near the great city".
en_revised: Traveling southeast from Matipura (末底補羅國) for more than four hundred li, one arrives at the country of Goviṣāṇa (瞿毘霜那國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Goviṣāṇa is over two thousand li in circuit. The capital city is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit; it is high, precipitous, and strategically secure, with a dense and prosperous population, and flowery groves and ponds are interspersed throughout. The climate and soil are the same as in the country of Matipura. The customs are simple and honest, and the people are diligent in learning and fond of merit. Many believe in non-Buddhist paths and seek present-day happiness. There are two saṃghārāmas with over one hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). There are more than thirty Deva temples, where followers of various paths live together. In the old saṃghārāma beside the great city, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王) that is over two hundred feet high. In the past, the Tathāgata stayed here for one month to preach the essential Dharma; nearby are the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. Beside these are two stūpas containing the hair and nail clippings of the Tathāgata, each over one zhang high.
li_quote: In an old monastery beside the capital city there is a stupa

issues: 如來在昔為龍王七日於此說法: 為 is "for" — the Tathāgata preached to the dragon king for seven days; he was not himself a dragon king in a former life.
en_revised: From here, traveling southeast for more than four hundred li, one reaches the country of Ahicchattra (堊醯掣呾邏國) (in the region of Central India). The country of Ahicchattra is more than three thousand li in circuit. The capital city is seventeen or eighteen li in circuit; it is situated in a secure and rugged position, is suitable for grain and wheat, and has many forests and springs. The climate is temperate and pleasant, and the customs of the people are honest and simple. They delight in the Way and are diligent in their studies, being talented and widely learned. There are more than ten sanghārāmas (伽藍) and over one thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Sammatiya school (正量部) of the Lesser Vehicle. There are nine deva temples, and more than three hundred sectarians who serve Īśvara (自在天) and are followers of the ash-smearing ascetics. Outside the city, beside a dragon pool, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). It was here that the Tathāgata in the past preached the Dharma for the dragon king for seven days. Beside it are four small stūpas, which are the sites of the remains of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas.
li_quote: Formerly the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for the dragon of this place for seven days.
