issues: 便詣華宮 is Kusumapura (拘蘇磨補羅，唐言花宮, named just before), not "the magnificent palace"; 集諸異學，商確微言 is the scholars of the various schools (the assembly fed 沙門 and 婆羅門), not "heterodox scholars" only.
en_revised: The country of Kanyākubja (羯若鞠闍國) is over four thousand li in circumference. The capital city borders the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) to the west; it is over twenty li in length and four to five li in breadth. The city moats and ramparts are solid and steep, with towers and pavilions facing one another, and flower groves and ponds that are bright and clear as mirrors. Rare goods from distant regions are mostly gathered here. The inhabitants are prosperous and happy, and their households are wealthy and abundant. Flowers and fruits are plentiful, and crops are sown in their proper seasons. The climate is harmonious and mild, and the customs are honest and simple. The people are refined in appearance and wear bright and elegant clothing. They are devoted to learning and skilled in the arts, and their discourse is clear and profound. Regarding the two paths of the heterodox and the orthodox, the number of believers is about equal. There are over one hundred saṅghārāmas and more than ten thousand monks, who study both the Great and Small Vehicles with equal diligence. There are over two hundred deva temples, and several thousand followers of heterodox paths.  In the age when the people of the country of Kanyākubja enjoyed long lives, the old capital city was called Kusumapura (拘蘇磨補羅) (In the language of the Tang, this means "Flowery Palace"). The king was named Brahmadatta (梵授); he possessed the accumulated merits of wisdom and virtue, was fully accomplished in both civil and military affairs, his power intimidated Jambudvīpa, and his fame shook neighboring countries. He had a full thousand sons, who were wise, brave, magnanimous, and resolute; he also had one hundred daughters, who were beautiful in appearance and refined in manner.  At that time, there was a rishi living by the side of the Gaṅgā who concentrated his spirit in meditative absorption for tens of thousands of years until his form resembled a withered tree. Migratory birds perched and gathered there, dropping a nyagrodha fruit upon the rishi's shoulder; as summers went and winters came, it cast a shade and grew to the size of an arch. After many years had passed, he rose from his meditation and wished to remove the tree, but fearing he might overturn the birds' nests, he desisted. The people of the time praised his virtue and called him the "Rishi of the Big Tree." The rishi cast his eyes along the riverbank and wandered through the thickets, where he saw the king’s daughters playing together. Desire for the world of the senses arose, and a heart of attachment was born; he then went to the Flowery Palace (Kusumapura), wishing to make a formal request. When the king heard the rishi had arrived, he went to welcome him in person and greeted him, saying, "The great rishi dwells in spirit beyond the material world; what has prompted this sudden visit?" The rishi said, "I have dwelt in the forest and marshes for many years. Emerging from meditation to wander, I saw the king’s daughters, and a heart of attachment was born; I have come from afar to make a request." Hearing these words, the king was at a loss for a plan and said to the rishi, "Return now to your dwelling; please wait for an auspicious day." The rishi heard this command and returned to the forest and marshes. The king then asked each of his daughters in turn, but none would consent to the marriage. Fearing the rishi’s power, the king became sorrowful and haggard. His youngest daughter, waiting for a break in the king’s affairs, calmly asked, "Father, you have a full thousand sons and ten thousand nations admire your transformation; for what reason are you so sorrowful, as if you are in fear?" The king said, "The Rishi of the Big Tree (Mahāvṛkṣa-ṛṣi) has deigned to seek a marriage alliance, yet none of you sisters are willing to obey. An immortal possesses great power and can bring about either disaster or fortune; if his heart’s desire is not met, he will surely fall into a rage, destroying the kingdom, ending our ancestral sacrifices, and bringing shame upon the late kings. Deeply contemplating this calamity, I am truly afraid." The youngest daughter replied, "To have caused this deep sorrow is our fault. I am willing to offer my humble self to preserve the prosperity of the state." Hearing this, the king was overjoyed; he ordered a carriage to be prepared and sent her to him. Upon arriving at the hermit’s hut, the king thanked the hermit, saying, "The great hermit has condescended from his transcendent state to show concern for worldly affairs; I dare to offer my young daughter to serve you by sweeping and cleaning." The hermit saw her and was displeased, saying to the king, "You slight this old man by matching me with one so unattractive." The king replied, "I have asked all my daughters, and none were willing to obey. Only this young one is willing to serve as a maid." The hermit, harboring anger, uttered a wicked curse: "May the ninety-nine daughters all have their waists bent at once; their forms being thus ruined and spoiled, they shall have no marriage for their entire lives." The king sent someone to verify this, and indeed, their backs were already hunched. From that time on, it has been called the City of the Hunchbacked Maidens (Kanyakubja).  The present king is of the Vaiśya caste, and his name is Harṣavardhana (translated into Chinese as "Increment of Happiness"). He rules over the land, the third king of two generations. His father’s name was Prabhākaravardhana (translated into Chinese as "Increment of Light"), and his elder brother’s name was Rājyavardhana (translated into Chinese as "Increment of the Kingdom"). Rājyavardhana succeeded to the throne as the eldest and governed with virtue. At that time, King Śaśāṅka (translated into Chinese as "Moon") of the kingdom of Karṇasuvarṇa (translated into Chinese as "Golden Ear") in East India often said to his ministers, "To have a virtuous ruler in a neighboring state is a misfortune for one's own country." Thereupon, he lured and invited him, and at the meeting, he killed him. Once the people had lost their ruler, the country fell into chaos. At that time, the high minister Bhaṇi (translated into Chinese as "Eloquent and Wise"), whose position and reputation were of great weight, said to the officials and the populace, "The great plan for the country must be decided this day." "The son of the former king and younger brother of the deceased monarch is benevolent by nature and filial by heart; he is truly close to the virtuous, and I wish for him to succeed to the throne. What do you think of this matter? Each of you, speak your mind." The assembly all looked up to his virtue, and there was never any dissenting opinion. Thereupon, the assistant ministers and officials all exhorted him to take the throne, saying: "May the prince listen to us; the late king accumulated merits and cultivated virtues, gloriously possessing the mandate of the state. The succession reached Rājyavardhana, and we expected him to live out his full span of years; but his assistants were not good, and he abandoned his life at the hands of an enemy—this is a great shame for the country and the fault of us, your humble servants. Public opinion and the rumors of the time truly point to your brilliant virtue. If you were to grace the land and the territory, avenge your kin upon the enemy, wash away the shame of the country, and glorify the legacy of your father, what merit could be greater than this? We hope you will not decline!"  The prince said, "The matter of national succession has been a difficult one from ancient times to the present; the establishment of one in the position of a sovereign must be considered with great prudence. I am truly lacking in virtue, and now that my father and elder brother have been taken from me, if I were to be pushed to succeed to the great throne, would I be able to succeed in my duties? Although public opinion deems it appropriate, how could I forget my own insignificance? Now, on the bank of the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) river, there is an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩) which is highly responsive; I wish to go there to seek guidance."   He immediately went before the Bodhisattva's image and fasted to make his request. The Bodhisattva, moved by his sincerity, manifested his form and asked, "What do you seek, that you are so diligent and earnest?" The prince said, "I have only accumulated disasters; my benevolent father has passed away, and to add to this cruel punishment, my virtuous elder brother has been murdered. Reflecting on myself, I am lacking in virtue, yet the people of the country honor me and urge me to succeed to the great throne to glorify my father's legacy." "I am foolish and ignorant; how dare I hope for the holy decree!" The Bodhisattva replied, "In your former life, you were an āraṇyaka-bhikṣu (練若苾芻) in this forest, and you were diligent and unremitting. By the power of that merit, you have become this prince. Since the King of Karṇasuvarṇa (金耳國王) has destroyed the Buddha-dharma, you, in succeeding to the throne, should revive it; let compassion be your aim and sympathy dwell in your heart, and you will soon be the ruler of the five regions of India. If you wish to extend the prosperity of the state, you must follow my instructions; then, through hidden blessings, you will have no powerful enemies in the neighboring lands. Do not ascend the lion throne, and do not assume the title of Great King."  Thereupon, having received these instructions, he withdrew and assumed the throne, calling himself "The Prince" and taking the title Śīlāditya (尸羅阿迭多) (in the language of Tang, this means "Sun of Precepts"). He then said to his ministers, "The vengeance for my brother has not been requited, and the neighboring countries have not submitted; I shall not have a moment to eat with my right hand. Let all you officials be of one mind and exert your strength." He then gathered the national troops and trained his soldiers. He had 5,000 elephant troops, 20,000 cavalry, and 50,000 infantry, and from the west to the east, he campaigned against those who would not submit. Without the elephants being unsaddled or the men removing their armor, he brought the five regions of India into submission within six years. Having expanded his territory, he further increased his military forces, reaching 60,000 elephant troops and 100,000 cavalry. For nearly thirty years, the weapons of war were not raised, and the government and teachings were peaceful. He devoted himself to frugality, cultivated merit and goodness, and forgot both sleep and food. He ordered that no meat be eaten throughout the five regions of India, and if anyone took a life, they would be executed without pardon. Along the banks of the Ganges (gaṅgā), he erected several thousand stūpas, each over one hundred feet high. In the cities, villages, thoroughfares, and crossroads of the five regions of India, he established hospices (精廬) stocked with food, drink, and medicine to be distributed to travelers and the poor, providing for them without ceasing. At every site of a sacred relic, he built a monastery (saṅghārāma). Every five years, he held a great pan-charity assembly (pañcavārṣika), emptying the royal treasury to bestow gifts upon all beings, withholding only the weaponry from his charitable offerings. Every year, he gathered śramaṇas from various countries for a meeting lasting twenty-one days, during which he provided them with the four requisites, grandly decorated the Dharma seats and discussion halls, and had them engage in debate to assess their relative merits, praise the virtuous and criticize the evil, and demote the ignorant while promoting the enlightened. Those whose observance of the precepts was steadfast and whose moral character was profound were invited to ascend the lion seat, and the king would receive the Dharma from them in person. Those whose precepts were pure but whose learning was not grounded in the classics were merely treated with respect to show his veneration. Those who had no discipline and whose corrupt conduct was manifest were driven out of the country, as he did not wish to see or hear of them. If the minor rulers and assistant ministers of neighboring countries cultivated merit without ceasing and sought goodness without weariness, the king would take them by the hand to sit together and call them his "virtuous friends." If they were otherwise, he would not meet them face-to-face, and if there were matters to discuss, he would communicate only through the exchange of envoys. He toured the regions to inspect the customs of the people and did not have a fixed residence, building temporary huts wherever he stopped. Only during the three months of the rainy season did he cease traveling due to the heavy rains. At his temporary palaces, he would daily prepare fine meals to feed one thousand monks and five hundred Brahmins of various schools. He divided each day into three periods: one period for managing affairs and governing, and two periods for cultivating merit and practicing virtue. He was diligent and tireless, feeling that the day was never long enough. Initially, I had accepted an invitation from King Kumāra to travel from the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) to the country of Kāmarūpa (迦摩縷波國). At that time, King Śīlāditya (戒日王) was on a tour of inspection in the country of Kajuṅghira (羯朱嗢祇羅國) and commanded King Kumāra, saying: "You should come quickly with the guest śramaṇa from Nālandā (那爛陀) to attend the assembly." Thereupon, I went with King Kumāra to meet him. After King Śīlāditya had offered greetings, he asked: "From what country have you come, and what is it that you seek?" I replied: "I have come from the Great Tang (大唐國) to seek the Buddha-Dharma." The king asked: "In what direction does the Great Tang lie? What is the extent of the route, and how far is it from here?" I replied: "It lies more than several tens of thousands of *li* to the northeast of here; it is what you in India call the country of Mahācīna (摩訶至那國)." The king said: "I have heard that in the country of Mahācīna there is a Son of Heaven, the Prince of Qin (秦王天子), who was perceptive and wise in his youth and has become divinely martial in his maturity. In the past, when the previous dynasty fell into chaos, the land was divided and collapsed, weapons of war arose on all sides, and the masses were poisoned by suffering. The Prince of Qin, however, early on cherished far-reaching strategies, aroused great compassion, rescued all sentient beings, and pacified the world. His civilizing influence reached far and wide, and his virtuous grace extended to distant places; strange lands and foreign regions admired his transformation and declared themselves his subjects. The people, having received his protection and nurturing, all sing the 'Music of the Prince of Qin Breaking the Ranks' (秦王破陣樂). I have heard these elegant hymns for a long time now. Is the reputation of his magnificent virtue truly as it is said? Is the Great Tang this country?" I replied, 'It is. Cīna (至那) was the name of the country under former kings; Great Tang is the title of my sovereign's realm. Before he ascended the throne, he was called the Prince of Qin; now that he has assumed the succession, he is titled the Son of Heaven. When the fortune of the previous dynasty ended, the masses were without a master, weapons of war arose in chaos, and living beings were cruelly harmed. The Prince of Qin, endowed by Heaven with vast magnanimity, felt compassion in his heart; his majestic influence stirred and spread, the various violent factions were exterminated, the eight directions were pacified, and ten thousand nations came to pay tribute. He loves and nurtures the four forms of birth, reveres and honors the Three Jewels, lightens taxes and levies, and reduces punishments; yet the state’s resources are abundant, and the common people have no need for hidden shelters. His civilizing influence and great transformation are difficult to fully describe.' King Śīlāditya (戒日王) said, 'Magnificent! The living beings of that land are blessed to be moved by such a holy lord.'  At that time, King Śīlāditya was about to return to the city of Kanyākubja (曲女城) to hold a religious assembly, followed by hundreds of thousands of people on the southern bank of the Ganges (殑伽河). King Kumāra (拘摩羅王) followed with tens of thousands of people, residing on the northern bank. They divided the river between them and advanced by both land and water. The two kings led the way, escorted by the four divisions of the army; some sailed in boats, others rode elephants, beating drums, blowing conches, and playing string and wind instruments. After ninety days, they reached the city of Kanyākubja, located in the Great Flower Wood to the west of the Ganges. At that time, more than twenty kings of various countries, having previously received the summons, arrived with the eminent śramaṇas, brahmans, officials, and soldiers of their respective kingdoms to gather for the great assembly. The King had previously built a large monastery (saṃghārāma) on the west side of the river. To the east of the monastery, he erected a precious terrace over one hundred feet high, in which was a golden Buddha image equal in size to the King’s own body. To the south of the terrace, he built a precious altar as a place to bathe the Buddha image. Fourteen or fifteen li to the northeast of this, he constructed a separate temporary palace. It was then the month of the middle of spring. From the first day of the month until the twenty-first, he provided delicious food to all the śramaṇas and brahmans. From the temporary palace to the monastery, pavilions were built along the sides of the road, decorated with every ornament, where musicians remained stationed, playing elegant music in succession.  The King brought out a golden image from the temporary palace, hollow and embossed, over three feet in height; it was loaded onto a large elephant and covered with a precious canopy. King Śīlāditya (戒日王), dressed in the attire of Indra (帝釋), held a precious canopy and attended on the left, while King Kumāra (拘摩羅王) assumed the guise of Brahmā (梵王), holding a white fly-whisk and attending on the right. Five hundred elephant-mounted soldiers on each side, clad in armor, provided a protective escort, while a hundred great elephants preceded and followed the Buddha image, carrying musicians who played music and beat drums. King Śīlāditya scattered pearls, various jewels, and gold and silver flowers at every step as an offering to the Three Jewels. First, they proceeded to the precious altar to bathe the image with perfumed water; then the King personally carried the image and escorted it to the western terrace, offering tens of hundreds of thousands of jewels and kauśeya garments as offerings. At that time, only twenty-some śramaṇas were permitted to follow, while the various kings served as guards. Once the meal was finished, he gathered the scholars of the various schools to discuss subtle doctrines and clarify profound principles. As the sun approached dusk, the King returned to his temporary palace. In this manner, he escorted the golden image daily, with the procession following as before, until the day of the dispersal. Suddenly, a fire broke out on the great terrace, and smoke and flames began to rage at the gatehouse of the monastery. The King said: "I have exhausted the treasures of the nation to build this monastery in honor of my late father, so as to manifest his magnificent achievements; yet my lack of virtue has left me without protection, resulting in such a disaster—with such an omen of calamity, what is the use of living!" He then burned incense, made a respectful petition, and took a vow, saying: "By the grace of my past good deeds, I have become a king over all India; may the power of my merit extinguish this fire, and if there is no spiritual response, I shall lose my life from this moment forth!" He immediately exerted himself, leaped across the threshold of the gate, and as if by some force extinguishing it, the fire died out and the smoke vanished. The various kings witnessed this miracle and their awe and reverence increased. Afterward, the King’s expression remained unchanged and his speech was as usual; he asked the various kings: "Suddenly this disaster has occurred, burning and destroying the finished work; what is in your hearts, and what are your thoughts?" The various kings prostrated themselves, weeping in sorrow, and replied: "This magnificent achievement was hoped to be passed on to future generations; now that it is reduced to ashes in an instant, how can we not be grieved? Furthermore, the various heterodox scholars are rejoicing in their hearts!" The King said: "Viewing it from this perspective, what the Tathāgata said is true. The heterodox scholars and those of different doctrines cling to the view of permanence, whereas only our Great Master teaches impermanence. However, my giving and renunciation have already been completed, and my heart’s desire has been fulfilled. Encountering this destruction, I have come to know once again the truthful teaching of the Tathāgata; this is a great good, and there is no reason for deep sorrow." Thereupon, he followed the various kings to the east to ascend the great stūpa to view the surroundings. Just as he was descending the steps, a strange man suddenly appeared holding a blade to confront the King. The King, in that moment of peril, retreated up the steps, bent down to seize the man, and handed him over to his officials. At that time, the officials were in a state of panic and did not know how to advance to rescue him. The various kings all requested that this man be executed, but King Śīlāditya (戒日王) showed no sign of anger and merely ordered that he not be killed. The King personally asked, "What have I done to wrong you that you would commit such a violent and evil act?" He replied, "Your Majesty’s virtuous grace is impartial, and both within and without the realm, all are indebted to you. However, I am mad and foolish; without considering the grander scheme, I was moved by a single word from the heretics to become an assassin and plot this treasonous murder." The King asked, "For what reason did the heretics harbor such evil intentions?" He replied, "Your Majesty has assembled the various nations and emptied the treasury to provide offerings to the śramaṇas and to cast Buddha images, yet the heretics, who were summoned from afar, have not been granted an audience; they truly feel ashamed and humiliated. This led me, in my madness and folly, to dare to commit this violent deception." Thereupon, the King investigated the followers of the heretics. There were five hundred Brahmins, all of them men of high talent, who had assembled by royal command; envious of the śramaṇas receiving the King's respect and honors, they shot fire-arrows to burn the precious terrace, hoping that in the ensuing chaos as people rushed to put out the fire, they could kill the Great King. Having found no other opportunity, they hired this man to rush into the narrow passage and carry out the assassination. At that time, the various kings and ministers requested that the heretics be executed, but the King only punished the ringleaders, left the remaining partisans unpunished, and banished the five hundred Brahmins from the borders of India. Thereupon, he returned to the capital.  To the northwest of the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata spent seven days here preaching various wonderful Dharmas. Beside it are the traces of where the four past Buddhas sat and walked. There are also small stūpas containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata.  To the south of the preaching stūpa, overlooking the Ganges (殑伽河) river, there are three monasteries (saṃghārāma) sharing the same wall but having separate gates; the Buddha images are magnificent and beautiful, the monastic community is solemn and respectful, and they employ several thousand households of monastery servants (淨人). In the precious casket of the *vihāra* (精舍) is a tooth of the Buddha, over an inch and a half long, of extraordinary luster and changing colors, shifting from morning to evening. People from near and far flock there, and the gentry and commoners gather in great numbers, daily numbering a hundred thousand, to perform acts of veneration. Because the overseers were troubled by the noise and confusion, they provisionally established a heavy tax, announcing to those near and far: "Those who wish to see the Buddha's tooth must pay a large sum of gold." Nevertheless, the number of those coming to pay homage remained vast, and they were happy to compete in their hearts to pay the gold tax. On every fast day, it is brought out and placed on a high seat; hundreds of thousands of people burn incense and scatter flowers, and although the flowers pile up, the tooth casket is never submerged.  To the left and right in front of the monasteries, there is a *vihāra*, each over a hundred feet high, with stone foundations and brick chambers; the Buddha images within are adorned with various jewels, some cast in gold or silver, others smelted from brass (鍮石). In front of each of the two *vihāra*s is a small monastery. Not far to the southeast of the monastery, there is a large *vihāra* (精舍) with stone foundations and brick chambers, over two hundred feet in height. Inside is a standing image of the Tathāgata, over thirty feet high, cast in brass (鍮石) and adorned with various wonderful jewels. On the stone walls surrounding the *vihāra*, the deeds experienced by the Tathāgata while practicing the bodhisattva path are carved and painted, fully and exhaustively engraved. Not far to the south of the stone *vihāra*, there is a temple to the Sun God (Āditya-deva). Not far to the south of that temple, there is a temple to Maheśvara (大自在天). Both are polished with blue stone and are equally exhaustive in their carvings; their scale and dimensions are the same as the Buddha’s *vihāra*. Each has a thousand households assigned to sweep and clean them, with drums, music, and singing continuing day and night without cessation. Six or seven li to the southeast of the great city, on the south bank of the Gaṅgā (殑伽河), there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata spent six months here speaking on the impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and impurity of the body. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. There are also small stūpas containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata; when people are afflicted with illness, if they circumambulate them with utmost sincerity, they will certainly be cured and receive their blessings.
li_quote: So he went to Kusumapura to ask to marry one of the king’s daughters.

issues: 外道曰：「我是誰？」 asks who Deva's "I" is ("Who is 'I'?"), not "Who am I?" (twice); the circle depends on it.
en_revised: From here, traveling southeast for more than seven hundred li, crossing to the south of the Ganges (Gaṅgā) and the north of the Yamunā, one reaches the country of Prayāga (鉢邏耶伽國) (in the territory of Central India). The country of Prayāga is more than five thousand li in circuit. The great capital city of the country is situated at the confluence of the two rivers and is more than twenty li in circuit. The crops are abundant and lush, and the fruit trees are thick and spreading. The climate is harmonious and pleasant, and the customs are virtuous and compliant. The people are fond of learning the arts and believe in non-Buddhist paths. There are two monasteries with few monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). There are several hundred deva temples, and the followers of non-Buddhist paths are very numerous.  To the southwest of the great city, in a forest of Campaka (瞻博迦) flowers, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). Although the base has collapsed and sunk, it is still more than one hundred feet high. In the past, the Tathāgata subdued non-Buddhists at this place. Beside it are the stūpas of the hair and nails, as well as traces of his walking meditation. Beside the hair and nail stūpas is an old monastery; this is the place where the Bodhisattva Deva (提婆) (in the language of the Tang, "Heaven-Received") composed the *Śataśāstra-vaipulya* (廣百論) to frustrate the Lesser Vehicle and subdue the non-Buddhists.  Formerly, when the Bodhisattva Deva came to this monastery from South India, there was a non-Buddhist Brahmin in the city who was renowned for his lofty arguments and possessed unimpeded eloquence; he would scrutinize names to demand their reality and use counter-interrogations to exhaust his opponents' words. Knowing that Deva was widely versed in profound mysteries and wishing to blunt his edge, he followed the name and asked, "What is your name?" Deva replied, "My name is Heaven (Deva)." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who is Heaven?" Deva replied, "Me." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who is 'I'?" Deva replied, "A dog." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who is the dog?" Deva replied, "You." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who are you?" Deva replied, "Heaven (Deva)." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who is Heaven?" Deva replied, "Me." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who is 'I'?" Deva replied, "A dog." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who is the dog?" Deva replied, "You." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who are you?" Deva replied, "Heaven." Through this cycle, the non-Buddhist finally attained realization. From that time forward, he deeply respected his noble conduct.
li_quote: The heretic said, “Who is I?” Deva said, “A dog.”

issues: 親友諫喻，其志不移。遂布衣服，遍周樹下: it is the relatives and friends who spread their clothes under the tree (and so save him), not the man himself.
en_revised: In the city there is a temple to a deity, adorned and resplendent, with many varied manifestations of spiritual power. According to its scriptures, this place is a supreme site for sentient beings to cultivate merit; to donate a single coin at this temple yields merit exceeding a gift of a thousand gold pieces elsewhere. Furthermore, those who treat life lightly and end their existence within the temple receive heavenly bliss and joy, eternal and inexhaustible. In front of the temple hall stands a large tree with luxuriant branches and dense foliage, where a man-eating ghost (piśāca) has made its home; consequently, many skeletal remains lie scattered around it. When people come to this temple, they invariably throw away their lives, being both intimidated by perverse doctrines and enticed by the deity; from antiquity to the present, this erroneous practice has continued without change. Recently, there was a Brahmin, a son of a noble clan, who was magnanimous, wise, perceptive, and highly talented; he came to the temple and said to the crowd: "It is difficult to guide and transform those with crooked customs and base minds; I shall first join them in their actions and then lead them to conversion." Having ascended the tree, he looked down and said to his friends: "I am about to die. What I once considered a deception is now proven true; heavenly beings and celestial music are in the sky to receive me, and I shall abandon this base form to follow them to a superior realm." He immediately sought to cast himself down to end his life, and though his friends remonstrated with him, his resolve did not waver. They then spread out their clothes all around beneath the tree, and when he threw himself down, he remained unharmed and his body was preserved. After a long while he regained consciousness and said: "I only saw various deities in the sky summoning me; this was the lure of evil spirits, not the attainment of heavenly bliss."
li_quote: They spread their garments on the ground below the tree and saved his life when he dropped to the ground.

issues: 一手一足執柱端，躡傍杙: one hand grips the top of the pillar and one foot treads on a side peg; the en has hand and foot both gripping the top.
en_revised: To the east of the great city, where two rivers meet, the area is over ten *li* wide; the land is high and dry, covered with fine sand. From ancient times to the present, whenever kings and noble families have wished to perform acts of charity, they have all come to this place to distribute gifts without measure, and thus it is called the Grand Arena of Almsgiving (Mahādānapīṭha). The current King Śīlāditya (戒日王) continues the traditions of his predecessors and is devoted to the practice of charity; he accumulates wealth for five years and then, in a single day, empties his stores, gathering a vast quantity of precious goods at this arena. On the first day, a large statue of the Buddha is installed and adorned with various gems, and the most exquisite and rare treasures are offered to it. Next, offerings are made to the resident monks; then to the assembly present; then to those of high talent and profound learning, and those of broad knowledge and many skills; then to the disciples of non-Buddhist sects and those who live in seclusion; and finally to the widowed, the orphaned, the solitary, and the poor and destitute. Every kind of precious object is prepared and the finest foods are exhausted; in this graded order, everyone is provided for. Once the treasury is emptied and all clothing and ornaments are exhausted, he gives away the lustrous pearl in his topknot and the various necklaces on his body one after another, without the slightest regret. Having completed the distribution, he declares: "How joyful! All that I possessed has now been deposited into the indestructible treasury of the Vajra." Following this, the kings of various countries each offer him precious garments, and within ten days, his treasury is filled once again. At the confluence of the rivers to the east of the Grand Arena of Almsgiving, several hundred people drown themselves every day. The local custom holds that those who wish to be reborn in heaven should abstain from food and drown themselves at this spot, for by bathing in the middle of the current, their sins and defilements will be eradicated. For this reason, people from distant foreign lands flock here, fasting for seven days before ending their lives. As for the mountain apes and wild deer, they roam in groups along the riverbank; some return after washing in the current, while others fast until they die. During the great almsgiving of King Śīlāditya (戒日王), there was a macaque that lived by the riverbank, remaining alone under a tree, isolating itself and fasting, until it died of starvation after several days. Therefore, the various non-Buddhist ascetics (外道) who practice austerities plant tall pillars in the river. At the approach of dawn, they climb them, one hand grasping the top of the pillar and one foot treading on a side peg, with the other hand and foot suspended and stretched out into the void, held straight without bending. They crane their necks and stare with wide eyes, watching the sun as it rotates to the right, and only when dusk falls do they descend. There are dozens of such followers who, hoping through this diligent suffering to escape the cycle of birth and death, have never slackened for several decades.
li_quote: stand with one hand holding the top of the pole and one foot on a peg

issues: 精舍東百餘步: east of the image-hall (vihāra) in the old palace, not "the monastery".
en_revised: From here, traveling southwest into a great forest, one encounters ferocious beasts and wild elephants that attack travelers in herds; unless one has a large party, it is difficult to pass through. After traveling more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Kauśāmbī (憍賞彌國) (formerly called the country of Kausāmbi, which is incorrect; it is within the borders of Central India). The country of Kauśāmbī is over six thousand *li* in circumference. The capital city is over thirty *li* in circumference. The soil is described as fertile, the land is rich in produce, and there is much *śāli* rice and abundant sugarcane. The climate is hot, and the customs of the people are fierce and impetuous. They are fond of learning and the arts, and they esteem and cultivate merit and goodness. There are more than ten *saṃghārāmas*, which are dilapidated and overgrown, with over three hundred monks who study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle. There are more than fifty *deva* temples, and the followers of non-Buddhist paths are very numerous. Within the old palace in the city, there is a large *vihāra* (精舍) over sixty feet high, housing a sandalwood Buddha image with a stone canopy suspended above it, which was made by King Udayana (鄔陀衍那王) (in the language of the Tang, "Giving Rise to Love"; formerly called King Youtian (優填王), which is erroneous). Miraculous signs appear from time to time, and divine light shines forth occasionally. Kings of various countries, relying on their strength, have wished to move it, but although they brought many people, none could shift it. Consequently, they have had copies made for worship, each claiming to have obtained the true likeness; when one speaks of their origin, it is indeed this very image. Initially, after the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment, he ascended to the heavenly palace to preach the Dharma for his mother, and for three months he did not return. The king, longing for him, wished to have his likeness made. He then requested the Venerable Maudgalyāyana to use his supernatural powers to transport an artisan to the heavenly palace to personally observe the Buddha's marvelous features and carve an image from sandalwood. When the Tathāgata returned from the heavenly palace, the sandalwood image rose to greet the World-Honored One, who consoled it, saying: "Have you been weary from the work of converting and guiding others? You are truly the hope for guiding those in the final age." More than one hundred paces to the east of the *vihāra* are the sites containing the traces of where the four past Buddhas sat and walked. Not far to the side are a well and a bathhouse used by the Tathāgata; the well still provides water for drawing, but the bathhouse has fallen into ruin.
li_quote: More than a hundred paces to the east of the temple are places where the four past buddhas used to sit

issues: 舉舍利子衣帶 / 解衣帶置地: the object is Śāriputra's robe-belt (衣帶), not "robe and belt" (the next sentences speak only of 此帶); 天祠，量等精舍…不蔽精舍…精舍之陰: the deva temple is compared with the vihāra just described (the "Shadow-covering Vihāra"), not "the monastery".
en_revised: Five or six *li* south of the city is the Jetavana (逝多林; in the language of the Tang, "Victory Grove"; the old term "Qituo" (祇陀) is a corruption), which is the Anāthapiṇḍada-ārāma (給孤獨園). The minister Sudatta (善施) of King Prasenajit (勝軍王) built a vihāra (精舍) for the Buddha; it was formerly a monastery, but now it lies in ruins. To the left and right of the east gate stand stone pillars over seventy feet high; the left pillar is topped with a carved wheel, and the right pillar is surmounted by the figure of a bull, both of which were erected by King Aśoka (無憂王). The buildings have collapsed, leaving only the old foundations, save for a single brick chamber that stands alone and intact, containing an image of the Buddha. Formerly, after the Tathāgata had ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother, King Prasenajit heard that King Udayana (出愛王) had carved a sandalwood image of the Buddha, and he thereupon had this image made. The Elder Sudatta was benevolent and intelligent; he accumulated wealth only to distribute it, rescuing the needy, relieving the poor, and showing compassion to the orphaned and the aged. People of the time praised his virtues and called him Anāthapiṇḍada ("the Giver to the Orphaned and Solitary"). Having heard of the Buddha’s merits, he developed a deep sense of reverence and wished to build a vihāra and invite the Buddha to descend. The World-Honored One commanded Śāriputra to accompany him to survey the land, and they found that only the garden of Prince Jeta (逝多太子) was high and dry. He immediately went to the Prince and explained his intentions in full. The Prince jokingly said, "If you cover the ground with gold, I will sell it." Upon hearing this, Sudatta’s heart was filled with joy; he immediately brought out his hidden gold and covered the ground as he had said. There was a small portion left uncovered, and the Prince requested to keep it, saying, "The Buddha is truly a fertile field; it is fitting to plant good seeds there." He then built the vihāra on the vacant land. The World-Honored One went there and said to Ānanda, "The garden ground was purchased by Sudatta (善施), and the trees were donated by Jeta (逝多); the two men were of one mind, and thus they jointly established this meritorious work. From now on, this place shall be called the Jetavana-anāthapiṇḍikārāma (逝多林給孤獨園)."  To the northeast of the Jetavana-anāthapiṇḍikārāma is a stūpa, which is the place where the Tathāgata washed a sick bhikṣu. Formerly, when the Tathāgata was in the world, there was a sick bhikṣu who was suffering and living alone. The World-Honored One saw him and asked, "What is your suffering? Why do you live alone?" He replied, "I am by nature lazy and cannot endure nursing the sick; therefore, I am now afflicted with illness, and there is no one to look after me." At that time, the Tathāgata felt compassion and said to him, "Good man, I will now nurse you." He stroked him with his hand, and his illness and suffering were all healed. He helped him out of the room, changed his bedding, personally washed him, and put new clothes on him. The Buddha said to the bhikṣu, "You should be diligent and exert yourself." Hearing this instruction, he felt gratitude, and his heart was joyful and his body at ease.  To the northwest of the Jetavana-anāthapiṇḍikārāma is a small stūpa, which is the place where Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅) exercised his supernatural power to lift Śāriputra’s (舍利子) robe-belt, but could not move it. Formerly, when the Buddha was at Lake Anavatapta (無熱惱池), humans and devas had all gathered, but only Śāriputra did not arrive at the assembly in time. The Buddha ordered Maudgalyāyana to go and summon him to join the gathering. Maudgalyāyana accepted the command and went; Śāriputra was mending his dharma-robe. Maudgalyāyana said, "The World-Honored One is now at Lake Anavatapta and has ordered me to summon you." Śāriputra (舍利子) said, "Wait a moment; I must finish mending this, and then I will go with you." Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅) said, "If you do not go quickly, I shall use my supernatural power to lift your stone chamber and take it to the great assembly." Śāriputra then untied his belt, placed it on the ground, and said, "If you can lift this belt, my body might move." At that time, Maudgalyāyana exerted his great supernatural power, but he could not lift the belt, and the earth shook because of it. He then used his supernatural foot-power to return to the place of the Buddha, where he saw that Śāriputra was already seated in the assembly. Maudgalyāyana bowed his head and sighed, saying, "Only now do I know that the power of supernatural abilities is not equal to the power of wisdom."  Not far from the stupa of the belt, there is a well. When the Tathāgata (如來) was in the world, water was drawn from it for the Buddha’s use. Beside it is a stupa built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which contains relics of the Tathāgata. The sites of his walking meditation and the places where he preached the Dharma are all marked with signs and have stupas built upon them. Dark spirits guard and protect them, and miraculous signs appear from time to time; sometimes heavenly music is played, and sometimes divine incense is smelled. The auspicious omens of these blessings are difficult to describe in full.  Not far behind the monastery is the place where the non-Buddhist ascetics (外道梵志) murdered a courtesan to slander the Buddha. The Tathāgata possesses the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the omniscience of all modes; he is revered by humans and devas, and honored by sages and worthies. At that time, the various non-Buddhists consulted together, saying, "We should employ deceit and slander him in the midst of the assembly." They then enticed and hired a courtesan, pretending she was coming to listen to the Dharma, and once this was known to the assembly, they secretly murdered her, buried her corpse beside a tree, and complained to the king, claiming injury. The king ordered a search, and her body was found in the Jetavana (逝多園). At that time, the non-Buddhists loudly proclaimed: "The great śramaṇa Gautama (喬答摩) always praises precepts and patience; now he has had illicit relations with this woman and killed her to silence her. Having committed both lechery and murder, where are his precepts and where is his patience?" The devas in the sky responded in unison, saying: "The wicked non-Buddhists have fabricated this slander."  More than one hundred paces to the east of the monastery is a large, deep pit; this is the place where Devadatta (提婆達多), intending to harm the Buddha with poison, fell alive into hell. Devadatta (in Chinese, "Heaven-bestowed") was the son of King Droṇodana (斛飯王). He practiced diligently for twelve years and had already memorized the eighty thousand sections of the Dharma-store. Later, for the sake of profit, he sought to learn supernatural powers and associated with evil friends, consulting with them: "My physical marks are thirty; they are not much less than the Buddha's. With the great assembly surrounding me, how am I different from the Tathāgata?" Having thought this, he proceeded to cause a schism in the Sangha. Śāriputra (舍利子) and Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子), following the Buddha’s instructions and relying on the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, preached and admonished them, and the Sangha was reconciled. Devadatta did not abandon his evil heart; he placed a deadly poison under his fingernails, intending to harm the Buddha while performing an act of homage. As he was carrying out this plot, coming from afar and arriving at this spot, the earth suddenly split open, and he fell alive into hell. To the south of this, there is another large pit where the Bhikṣu Kokālika (瞿伽梨) fell alive into hell for slandering the Tathāgata. More than eight hundred paces to the south of the pit of Kokālika, there is a large, deep pit, which is the place where the Brahmin woman Ciñcā (戰遮) fell alive into hell for slandering the Tathāgata. When the Buddha was preaching the essentials of the Dharma to humans and devas, a disciple of an external path saw from afar the great assembly paying homage to the World-Honored One and thought to herself, "I must humiliate Gautama (喬答摩) today and ruin his good reputation, so that my teacher alone may possess a fragrant name." She then concealed a wooden basin tied to her body and went to the Jetavana (給孤獨園), where she cried out in a loud voice amidst the great assembly, "This preacher has had illicit relations with me, and the child in my womb is of the Śākya clan." Those of evil views all believed it to be true, while those who were steadfast knew it to be a slander. At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra (天帝釋), wishing to dispel the doubt, transformed into a white mouse and gnawed through the cord holding the basin. The sound of the cord snapping startled the great assembly, and all who saw and heard it felt their joy increase. One person in the assembly stood up, held the wooden basin, and showed it to the woman, saying, "Is this your child?" At that moment, the earth split open of its own accord, and she fell into it, her whole body sinking into the Avīci (無間) hell to suffer the full consequences of her actions. These three pits are bottomless; during the heavy rains of autumn and summer, when ditches and pools overflow, no water ever remains in these deep hollows. Sixty or seventy paces to the east of the monastery, there is a vihāra (精舍) over sixty feet high, in which there is an image of the Buddha seated facing east. In the past, the Tathāgata debated with various heretics here. To the east, there is a deva temple equal in size to the vihāra. When the sun rises and sheds its light, the shadow of the deva temple does not cover the vihāra; when the sun is about to set, the shadow of the vihāra covers the deva temple. Three or four li to the east of the Shadow-covering Vihāra (影覆精舍), there is a stūpa, which is the place where the Venerable Śāriputra debated with the heretics.  Initially, the elder Sudatta (善施長者) purchased the garden of Prince Jeta (逝多太子) and wished to build a monastery for the Tathāgata. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra accompanied the elder to survey the site. The teachers of the six heretical schools sought to compete in supernatural powers, but Śāriputra converted them according to the circumstances and subdued them in response to their challenges. Beside it, in front of a vihāra, a stūpa has been built; here the Tathāgata defeated the various heretics and also accepted the invitation of Mother Viśākhā.  To the south of the stūpa where he accepted the invitation is the place where King Virūḍhaka (毘盧釋迦王) (formerly called King Piliuli (毘琉離主), which is incorrect) raised an army to slaughter the Śākya clan, and where he saw the Buddha and turned his troops back. After King Virūḍhaka ascended the throne, he pursued his resentment over a previous humiliation, raised an army, and mobilized the masses. Once the deployment was complete, he issued the order to march. At that time, a bhikṣu heard of this and informed the Buddha. The World-Honored One then sat beneath a withered tree. King Virūḍhaka saw the World-Honored One from afar, dismounted to pay his respects, stood back, and said, "Lush trees are spreading and thick; why do you not sit under them, but instead stay by a withered stump and rotten branches?" The World-Honored One replied, "One's own kin are like the branches and leaves. When the branches and leaves are in danger, where is the shade?" The King said, "The World-Honored One is doing this for his kinsmen; I may turn back my carriage." Thereupon, seeing the Holy One and feeling moved, he returned his army to his country. Beside the place where the army turned back, there is a stūpa, which is the place where the Śākya women were slaughtered. When King Virūḍhaka (毘盧釋迦王) had conquered the Śākyas, he selected five hundred women to fill his palace. The Śākya women were filled with indignation and, speaking resentful and insolent words, cursed the King, saying, "You are the son of a domestic servant." When the King heard this, he became enraged and ordered them to be slaughtered. The executioners obeyed the King’s command, severed their hands and feet, and threw them into a pit. At that time, the Śākya women, enduring their suffering, called upon the Buddha. The World-Honored One, with his holy insight, perceived their bitter agony and commanded the bhikṣus to gather their robes and go there. He preached the subtle Dharma to the Śākya women, explaining how they were bound by the five desires, wandering through the three evil paths, separated from those they loved, and caught in the long cycle of birth and death. When the Śākya women heard the Buddha’s instruction, they cast off the dust and removed the stains, attained the pure Dharma-eye, and at that same moment passed away and were all reborn in the heavens. At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra transformed himself into a Brahmin, collected their remains, and cremated them; later generations have commemorated this. Not far from the stūpa of the slaughtered Śākyas, there is a large dried-up pond, which is the place where King Virūḍhaka sank into the earth and fell into hell. After the World-Honored One had observed the Śākya women, he returned to the Jetavana (給孤獨園) and told the bhikṣus, "Seven days from now, King Virūḍhaka will be consumed by fire." When the King heard the Buddha’s prophecy, he was filled with great fear and anxiety. When the seventh day arrived, he was safe and without danger. The king, feeling jubilant, ordered the palace maidens to go to the riverside to enjoy themselves with music and wine. Still fearing that a fire might break out, he rowed upon the clear currents and drifted along with the waves. Suddenly, a blazing fire erupted, consuming the light boat; the king’s body fell, and he entered the Avīci Hell to undergo all manner of suffering.

issues: 不書日月: the inscription gives no date (day and month), not "the year or month".
en_revised: Three or four *li* to the northwest of the city, one crosses the Ajitavatī River (阿恃多伐底河) (in the Tang language, "Invincible"; this is merely the common name in this world. The old name, Alilobati River (阿利羅跋提河), is a corruption. The classical language calls it the Hiraṇyavatī River, which translates as "River of Gold"). Not far from the west bank, one reaches the Sāla (娑羅) grove. The trees resemble the oak, but their bark is greenish-white and their leaves are very glossy and smooth. Four trees are particularly tall; this is the place where the Tathāgata attained extinction (parinirvāṇa). In the large brick vihāra (精舍) is an image of the Tathāgata in the state of *nirvāṇa*, lying with his head to the north. Beside it is a *stūpa* built by King Aśoka; although the base has collapsed and sunken, it is still over two hundred feet high. In front of it stands a stone pillar recording the event of the Tathāgata’s extinction; although there is an inscription, it does not record the day or month. I have heard from ancient records that the Buddha entered *parinirvāṇa* at the age of eighty on the fifteenth day of the second half of the month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the third month. The Sarvāstivāda school, however, holds that the Buddha entered *parinirvāṇa* on the eighth day of the second half of the month of Kārttika, which corresponds to the eighth day of the ninth month. Since the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*, the various schools have held differing opinions: some say more than 1,200 years have passed, some say more than 1,300 years, some say more than 1,500 years, and others say more than 900 but less than 1,000 years. Not far from the side of the vihāra is a *stūpa* marking the place where the Tathāgata, when practicing the Bodhisattva path, acted as the king of a flock of pheasants to save them from a fire. Formerly, there was a great, dense forest in this place, where feathered and furred creatures nested and lived in burrows. Sudden winds arose from all directions, and the fierce flames surged rapidly. At that time, there was a pheasant who, moved by compassion, soaked its wings in a clear stream and flew into the air to sprinkle the water. The Heavenly Emperor Śakra (天帝釋) looked down and said to it, "Why are you so foolish, exhausting your wings in vain? A great fire has broken out, burning the forest and the wilderness; how could your tiny body possibly extinguish it?" The pheasant replied, "Who is it that speaks?" He said, "I am the Heavenly Emperor Śakra." The pheasant said, "Today, the Heavenly Emperor possesses great merit and power, and there is no desire he cannot fulfill; to relieve disasters and rescue those in distress should be as easy as pointing to one's own palm. Yet you instead question my lack of success—where does the blame truly lie? The fierce fire is currently raging; do not speak further!" It then flew off again to head toward the flowing water. The Heavenly Emperor then scooped up water with his hands and sprinkled it over the forest; the fire was extinguished and the smoke vanished, the lives of all creatures were saved, and thus it is now called the Fire-extinguishing Stūpa (救火窣堵波).  Not far from the side of the place where the pheasant extinguished the fire, there is a stūpa marking the place where the Tathāgata, while practicing the Bodhisattva path, saved lives as a deer. In the remote past, there was a great forest here; a fire broke out in the wilderness, and the birds and beasts were driven to desperation, facing the peril of a swift current in front and the hardship of a raging fire behind, such that none escaped drowning or losing their lives. The deer, moved by compassion, positioned its body across the current, its skin pierced and bones broken, forcing itself to rescue the drowning. A lame hare arrived last, and the deer, enduring its fatigue and pain, rescued it as well. When its strength was exhausted, it drowned and died. The devas gathered its remains and erected a stūpa. Not far to the west of where the deer rescued the drowning, there is a stūpa. This is the place where Subhadra (蘇跋陀羅) (in the Tang language, "Good and Virtuous" [善賢]; formerly called Xubatuoluo [須跋陀羅], which is incorrect) entered into extinction. This Good and Virtuous one was originally a Brahmin teacher. He was one hundred and twenty years old, an elder of great wisdom. Hearing that the Buddha was about to enter extinction, he arrived at the twin trees and asked Ānanda, "The Buddha, the World-honored One, is about to enter extinction. I have doubts and hesitations, and I wish to ask him questions." Ānanda said, "The Buddha is about to enter nirvāṇa; please do not disturb him." He replied, "I have heard that it is difficult to encounter a Buddha in the world and difficult to hear the true Dharma. I have deep doubts and fear that I will have no one to ask." Subhadra then entered and first asked the Buddha, "Are there various other groups who call themselves teachers, each having different doctrines, handing down instructions to guide the laity—can Gautama (formerly called Qutan [瞿曇], which is a corruption and abbreviation) know them all?" The Buddha said, "I have thoroughly investigated them all," and then he expounded them for him. Having heard this, Subhadra’s mind was purified and he gained faith and understanding. He requested to enter the Dharma and receive the full ordination. The Tathāgata said to him, "Are you able to do so? For those of other paths and different schools who wish to practice the holy life, they must be tested for four years. By observing their conduct and examining their nature—if their deportment is tranquil and their speech is truthful—then they may practice the holy life in my Dharma. It depends on the person's conduct; how could this be difficult?" Subhadra said, "The World-honored One is compassionate and merciful, bestowing salvation without partiality. If one is tested for four years, the three karmas will then be in accord." The Buddha said, "I have already said that it depends on the person's conduct!" Thereupon, Subhadra (善賢) renounced the household life, immediately received the full precepts, and diligently practiced with a courageous body and mind. Before long, he had no doubts regarding the Dharma and personally attained realization. Before the night was far advanced, he attained the fruit of an Arhat; all his outflows were exhausted, and his holy life was established. Unable to bear seeing the Buddha enter mahānirvāṇa, he entered the fire-element samādhi (火界定) amidst the assembly, manifested supernatural powers, and entered nirvana first. This was the Tathāgata's final disciple, who attained extinction first; he is the one who, in the past, was the hare that crossed the river last. Beside the spot where Subhadra entered nirvana, there is a stūpa; this is the place where the Vajra-holder (執金剛) fell to the ground.  The Greatly Compassionate World-honored One, having appeared to benefit beings according to their capacities, finished his work of transformation and entered the joy of extinction, lying down with his head to the north between the twin trees. When the Vajra-holding deity, the Guhyapāda Malla (密迹力士), saw the Buddha enter nirvana, he cried out in bitter grief: "The Tathāgata has forsaken me and entered mahānirvāṇa; I have no refuge and no protection; the poisoned arrow has struck deep, and the fire of sorrow burns fiercely!" He cast aside his vajra-club and fell to the ground in a swoon. After a long time, he rose again, filled with sorrow and longing, and they said to one another: "In the great ocean of birth and death, who will serve as the boat and oar? In the long night of ignorance, who will serve as the lamp and torch?" Beside the spot where the Vajra-holder fell to the ground, there is a stūpa; this is the place where the Tathāgata was venerated for seven days after his nirvana. When the Tathāgata was about to enter nirvana, a brilliant light shone everywhere. Humans and devas gathered in full, all feeling deep sorrow and emotion, saying to one another: "The Great Awakened World-Honored One is now about to enter nirvana; the merit of sentient beings is exhausted, and the world is left without a refuge." The Tathāgata lay on his right side on a lion-couch and addressed the great assembly: "Do not say that the Tathāgata has entered final nirvana. The Dharma-body is eternally abiding and free from all change. You should abandon sloth and seek liberation early." The bhikṣus sobbed and grieved. At that time, Aniruddha (阿泥𢫫陀) (𢫫 is read 盧骨反, i.e. *lu[t]*; formerly called Analü [阿那律], which is incorrect) told the bhikṣus: "Stop, stop! Do not grieve; the devas will mock and wonder at you." When the Malla people had finished their offerings and wished to lift the golden coffin to proceed to the cremation ground (涅疊般那), Aniruddha said: "Wait! The devas wish to keep it for seven days to make offerings." Thereupon, the host of devas held exquisite heavenly flowers, wandered through the void, praised the holy virtues, and each exhausted their sincere hearts to join in making offerings. Beside the place where the coffin rested, there is a stūpa; this is the spot where Lady Mahāmāyā wept for the Buddha. After the Tathāgata had entered nirvana and the encoffining was completed, Aniruddha ascended to the heavenly palace and informed Lady Mahāmāyā, saying: "The Great Holy Dharma King has now entered nirvana." Upon hearing this, Mahāmāyā was choked with grief and fainted. She went with the assembly of devas to the space between the twin trees, where she saw the saṃghāṭi (monastic robe), the pātra (alms bowl), and the khakkhara (pewter staff). Stroking them, she wailed in agony, fainting and then regaining her voice to cry out: "The merit of humans and devas is exhausted, and the Eye of the World is extinguished! Now these objects are empty and without a master." By the holy power of the Tathāgata, the golden coffin opened of its own accord, emitting a great light; he sat up with palms joined and consoled his compassionate mother: "You have descended from a great distance! All conditioned things are by nature such; I pray you, do not grieve so deeply." Ānanda, suppressing his sorrow, asked the Buddha: "If future generations ask me, how shall I answer them?" He replied: "Say that after the Buddha had entered nirvana, his compassionate mother Mahāmāyā descended from the heavenly palace to the space between the twin trees, and for the sake of unfilial sentient beings, the Tathāgata rose from his golden coffin and preached the Dharma with his palms joined."

issues: 為諸眾生分散舍利，唯有髮、爪儼然無損: for the sake of beings the relics were scattered (broke into fragments); only hair and nails stayed whole — not "in order to distribute the relics…only the hair and nails remained"; 初出臂，問阿難治路: he asked Ānanda about mending the road, not "about the path".
en_revised: Crossing the river more than three hundred paces to the north of the city, there is a stupa, which is the place where the Tathāgata (如來) was cremated. The ground is now yellow and black, the soil mixed with ash and charcoal; if one requests with utmost sincerity, one may obtain relics. When the Tathāgata entered into extinction, humans and devas were moved by grief; they made a coffin of the seven treasures and wrapped his body in a thousand layers of fine cotton, offered incense and flowers, and set up banners and canopies. The Malla (末羅) people then bore the hearse in a procession, with guides in front and followers behind, crossing the Gold River to the north, where they filled it with fragrant oil, piled up much scented wood, and set it ablaze. Two layers of the cotton did not burn: one that was closest to the body and one that covered the outermost layer. For the sake of all sentient beings the relics were scattered into fragments; only the hair and nails remained intact and undamaged. Beside the place of cremation is a stupa, marking the spot where the Tathāgata revealed his two feet to Mahākāśyapa (大迦葉波). When the Tathāgata’s golden coffin had been lowered and the fragrant wood piled up, the fire would not ignite, and the assembly was filled with alarm. Aniruddha (阿泥𢫫陀) said, "We must wait for Kāśyapa." At that time, Mahākāśyapa, with five hundred disciples, came from the mountain forests and arrived at the city of Kuśinagara (拘尸城). He asked Ānanda, "Can the body of the World-Honored One still be seen?" Ānanda replied, "It is wrapped in a thousand layers of fine cotton, enclosed in heavy coffins, and the fragrant wood has already been piled up; the cremation is about to take place." At that moment, the Buddha, from within the coffin, revealed his two feet; upon the wheel-marks, a strange color was visible. He asked Ānanda, "Why is there this color?" He replied, "When the Buddha first entered parinirvāṇa, humans and devas were overcome with grief, and the tears of the multitude splashed and stained it, causing this strange color." Kāśyapa paid homage, circumambulated, and offered praises; the fragrant wood ignited spontaneously, and a great fire blazed fiercely. Thus, when the Tathāgata entered extinction, he emerged from the coffin three times: first, he extended his arm to ask Ānanda about mending the road; next, he sat up to preach the Dharma for his mother; finally, he revealed his two feet to show them to Mahākāśyapa. Beside the place where he revealed his feet is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which is the site where the eight kings divided the relics. In front of it, a stone pillar was erected, inscribed with an account of the event. After the Buddha had entered nirvāṇa and the cremation was completed, the kings of eight countries arrived with their fourfold armies and dispatched a straightforward Brahmin to say to the Mallas of Kuśinagara (拘尸力士), "The Teacher of gods and men has entered extinction in this country; therefore, we have come from afar to request a share of the relics." The Mallas replied, "The Tathāgata descended in his majesty to this lower realm; here the bright guide of the world has been extinguished and we have lost the compassionate father of all living beings. The relics of the Tathāgata should naturally be worshipped by us alone; you have wearied yourselves on the road in vain, for you shall never obtain them." At that time, the various great kings requested them with humble words, but since they were not granted, they said again, "If polite requests are not followed, the might of our armies is not far off." The straightforward Brahmin spoke aloud, "Reflect! The Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One patiently cultivated merit and goodness throughout vast kalpas, as I presume you have all heard; it is not appropriate for you now to seek to oppress one another. Since the relics are here, they should be divided into eight equal portions so that each may receive them for worship; why go so far as to raise troops?" The Mallas followed his words and immediately measured the relics, intending to divide them into eight portions. Śakra (帝釋) said to the kings, "The heavens should have a share; do not rely on force to compete." The Nāga kings Anavatapta (阿那婆答多), Mucilinda (文隣), and Elāpattra (醫那鉢呾羅) also proposed, "Do not exclude us. If it comes to force, the masses are no match for us." The straightforward Brahmin said, "Do not clamor and contend; it is proper to divide them together." He immediately made three portions: first for the devas, second for the Nāga host, and third to remain among humans, which the eight kingdoms then subdivided. The devas, Nāgas, and human kings were all moved to sorrow.

issues: 沙門食訖，攝衣即語: the brahman's next words 向許有說，今何無言 show the monk did not speak; the sense is that he gathered his robe to leave (即路, as Li reads), not "and spoke".
en_revised: Traveling two hundred-odd *li* southwest from the relic stūpa, one arrives at a large town (大邑聚). There was a brāhmaṇa there, a man of great wealth and high standing, whose lineage was pure and unmixed, who had mastered the five sciences (pañcavidyā), and who deeply revered the Three Jewels. Adjacent to his residence, he established a monastery, exhausting his resources to provide it with every adornment. Whenever members of the saṅgha traveled along that road, he would earnestly invite them to stay, offering them his wholehearted support, whether they stopped for a single night or for as long as seven days. Later, when King Śaśāṅka (設賞迦王) destroyed the Buddha-dharma, the saṅgha was dispersed and the years passed quickly, yet the brāhmaṇa remained filled with sincere sorrow. While walking in meditation, he saw a śramaṇa with bushy eyebrows and white hair approaching, leaning on a staff. The brāhmaṇa hurried to welcome him, asked where he had come from, and invited him into the monastery, where he prepared every kind of offering, including a morning meal of porridge cooked with pure milk. The śramaṇa accepted it, but after tasting only a morsel, he set down his bowl and sighed deeply. The brāhmaṇa, holding the food, knelt and asked, "Great Virtuous One, whose wisdom and merit follow conditions, I am fortunate to have your presence; were you uncomfortable during the night, or was the porridge not to your taste?" The śramaṇa replied with compassion, "I grieve that the merit and blessings of sentient beings are gradually thinning. Let that matter rest for now; I will speak after I have eaten." Once the śramaṇa had finished eating, he adjusted his robes to set off. The brāhmaṇa said, "You previously promised to speak; why are you silent now?" The śramaṇa replied, "I have not forgotten. What I have to discuss is not easy, and the matter may invite doubt. If you truly wish to hear it, I shall now speak of it briefly." "What I sighed about just now was not to disparage your porridge. For several hundred years, I have not tasted such a flavor. Long ago, when the Tathāgata was in the world, I was in his retinue at the Bamboo Grove Monastery (Veṇuvana-vihāra) in the city of Rājagṛha, where I would lean over the clear stream to wash the vessels, or use the water for rinsing and bathing. Alas! The rich milk of today cannot compare to the plain water of old; this is because the merit of humans and devas has been exhausted." The brāhmaṇa asked, "In that case, does the Venerable One mean that you personally saw the Buddha?" The śramaṇa replied, "Indeed. Have you not heard of the Buddha’s son, Rāhula? I am he. To protect the True Dharma, I have not yet entered final extinction." Having said these words, he suddenly vanished. The brāhmaṇa then anointed and swept the room where he had stayed, set up an image with solemn ceremony, and paid his respects as if he were still present. Traveling further through the great forest for more than five hundred li, one arrives at the country of Vārāṇasī (婆羅痆斯國) (痆 is read 女黠反; formerly called Poluonai, which is incorrect. It is in the region of Central India).

en_revised: Two or three li to the southwest of the monastery, there is a stupa over three hundred feet high; its base is broad and imposing, adorned with lustrous and rare gems. It has no tiered niches on top, but is surmounted by an inverted bowl; although a central pillar was erected, it lacks the usual rings and bells. Beside it is a small stupa, marking the place where the five men, including Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya (阿若憍陳如), abandoned their restraint to welcome the Buddha.  Previously, after the Prince Sarvārthasiddha (薩婆曷剌他悉陀; in Tang language, "Accomplished in All Meanings"; formerly called Siddhārtha, which is an abbreviated and inaccurate rendering) had climbed over the city wall, he dwelt in mountain valleys, forgetting his own body in his devotion to the Dharma. King Śuddhodana then commanded three members of the royal clan and two from the maternal side, saying: "My son, Accomplished in All Meanings, has left home to practice and learn; he wanders alone through mountains and marshes and dwells in isolation among the woods and thickets. Therefore, I order you to follow him and keep track of his whereabouts. Internally, you are his uncles and maternal uncles; externally, he is your lord and you are his subjects. In all his movements, you should know when to advance and when to stop."  The five men accepted the command and kept watch over him, providing protection. Consequently, they practiced diligently, hoping to attain liberation. They often said to one another, "Is the path to enlightenment attained through suffering, or is it attained through ease?" Two of them said, "Ease is the path." Three of them said, "Hardship and suffering are the path." The two and the three argued with each other, unable to reach a clear conclusion. Thereupon, the Prince contemplated the ultimate truth and, in order to subdue the non-Buddhist ascetics, he restricted himself to a few grains of hemp and rice to sustain his body. Those two men saw this and said, "What the Prince is practicing is not the true Dharma." "The Way is to be realized through ease; now he practices diligent suffering, so he is not one of our kind." They abandoned him and fled to a distance, contemplating the realization of the fruit. The Prince practiced asceticism for six years without realizing enlightenment; wishing to verify that asceticism was not the truth, he accepted milk gruel and attained the fruit. These three men heard of this and sighed, saying, "His merit was on the verge of completion, yet now he has retreated. Six years of asceticism, and in one day he has cast away his merit!" Thereupon, they followed one another to seek out the two men. Having met, they sat upright and engaged in lofty discourse, discussing further: "Formerly we saw the Prince, Sarvārthasiddha (一切義成), leave the royal palace, go to the desolate valleys, discard his precious garments, and don deerskin. He applied himself with diligent resolve and painstaking integrity to seek the profound and wonderful Dharma, aspiring to the supreme fruit. Now he has accepted milk gruel from a cowherd girl, ruining his path and compromising his resolve; we know of it, and nothing can be done." Those two men said, "Why are you so late in seeing this? This is merely a reckless person. Dwelling in the deep palace, secure in his exalted status, he could not calm his mind; he fled to the mountain forests, abandoned the position of a wheel-turning king, and performed the acts of a base and lowly person—what is there to think about? Speaking of him only increases one's sorrow!" The Bodhisattva bathed in the Nairañjanā (尼連河) River, sat under the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree, attained perfect enlightenment, and was titled the Teacher of Gods and Humans. Remaining in silent tranquility, he observed those ready for deliverance and said, "That Udraka Rāmaputra (欝頭藍子) has realized the meditative state of neither perception nor non-perception and is capable of receiving the wonderful Dharma." The devas in the sky heard his voice and replied, "It has been seven days since Udraka Rāmaputra (欝頭藍子) passed away." The Tathāgata sighed with regret, "How unfortunate that he did not encounter this, for he was on the verge of hearing the wonderful Dharma, yet he has suddenly undergone transformation!" He observed the world again, seeking someone to teach, and found Ārāḍa Kālāma (阿藍迦藍), who had attained the meditative state of nothingness and could be taught the ultimate truth. The devas said again, "He passed away five days ago." The Tathāgata sighed once more, pitying his meager fortune. He observed carefully again: who was fit to receive instruction? Only the five men in the Deer Park (鹿林) could be guided first. At that time, the Tathāgata rose from the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree and headed for the Deer Park; his deportment was serene, his divine light shone brilliantly, his brow-hair possessed the luster of jade, and his body was the color of genuine gold as he proceeded composedly to guide those five men. When these five men saw the Tathāgata from afar, they said to one another, "Sarvārthasiddha (一切義成) is the one coming there. Much time has passed, he has not realized the holy fruit, and his aspirations have retreated, so he is coming to seek us. We should each remain silent and not rise to greet or pay homage to him." As the Tathāgata gradually approached, his divine power moved them; the five men, forgetting their resolve, bowed to welcome him with greetings and attended to him according to etiquette. The Tathāgata gradually guided them, revealing the wonderful truth to them, and when the rains retreat was over, they finally attained the realization of the fruit.
