issues: 感荷厚恩，忍不報語 and 以報厚德: the great kindness to be repaid is the hermit's (the hero is telling the hermit), not the former master's; the en twice gives it to "his".
en_revised: Going two or three li east from the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva), one reaches a stūpa. Beside it is a dried-up pond, more than eighty paces in circumference, known as "Life-saving" (Jīvitatrāṇa) and also called "Hero" (Vīra). According to the local records: several hundred years ago, there was a hermit who built a hut and lived in seclusion beside this pond. He was extensively learned in the arts and had mastered the ultimate divine principles, being able to turn rubble into jewels and change the forms of humans and animals, yet he was not yet able to ride the winds and clouds or join the company of the immortals. He examined the diagrams and studied the ancients, seeking further for the arts of immortality. The formula stated: "Immortality is the art of long life. If one wishes to seek this study, one must first settle one's resolve and build an altar more than one zhang in circumference. Command a man of mettle, renowned for his loyalty and courage, to hold a long sword and stand at the corner of the altar, holding his breath and remaining silent from dusk until dawn. The seeker of immortality shall sit in the center of the altar, hand resting on the long sword, chanting divine incantations, withdrawing his vision and turning his hearing inward; by daybreak, he shall ascend to immortality. The sharp sword he holds will turn into a precious blade; he will soar through the void and tread upon the air, reigning over the company of immortals, and with the sword in hand, he will command, and all he desires will be fulfilled, without decline or aging, without sickness or death." Having obtained this formula for immortality, the man traveled in search of a man of mettle, but despite seeking for many years, he could not find anyone to satisfy his wish. Later, in the city, he encountered a man wailing as he walked along the road. The hermit observed his appearance and was greatly delighted; he approached him and asked with concern, "Why are you so aggrieved and wounded?" The man replied, "I am poor and destitute, and I labor to support myself." His master had recognized his worth and placed deep trust in him, promising that when five years were completed, he would be rewarded with a heavy bounty. Consequently, he endured toil and hardship, forgetting his suffering. As the five years were about to conclude, he made a single mistake, and for this he was not only whipped and humiliated but also received nothing. "With this weighing on my heart, who is there to pity my grief?" The hermit bade him travel together, and they arrived at a thatched hut. By the power of his arts, the hermit conjured a spread of food and drink; afterwards, he ordered him to bathe in the pond, dressed him in new clothes, and presented him with five hundred gold coins, saying, "When these are exhausted, come and ask for more; pray do not treat me as an outsider." From that time on, the hermit repeatedly bestowed heavy gifts upon him, secretly performing acts of kindness to stir his heart. The hero (烈士) repeatedly sought to offer his life in service to repay the one who understood him. The hermit said, "I have sought a hero for many years; fortunately we have met, and your singular appearance matches the prophecies. I have no other motive; I only wish for you to remain silent for a single night." The hero replied, "I would not even refuse death, so how could I not merely hold my breath?" Thereupon, they set up an altar, received the immortal method, and followed the instructions to perform the rites, sitting and waiting for the sun to set. After dusk, each attended to his duties: the hermit recited divine incantations, while the hero gripped his sharp blade. When it was almost dawn, he suddenly let out a cry. At that moment, fire descended from the sky, and smoke and flames billowed like clouds. The hermit quickly pulled the man into the pond to escape the danger. Afterwards, he asked, "I warned you to remain silent; why did you cry out in alarm?" The hero replied, "After receiving your instructions, when midnight came, I fell into a trance-like dream, and strange transformations began to arise." I saw my former master come in person to comfort and thank me; mindful of your great kindness, I restrained myself and did not respond. He became furious and killed me. I entered the intermediate state (antarābhava) and, looking back at my corpse, sighed with regret, yet I still wished to remain silent throughout my lives to repay your great virtue. I was then reborn into a great Brahmin family in South India; from conception to birth and through all manner of hardships, I bore your grace and virtue in mind and never made a sound. Even when I reached the stages of schooling, capping, marriage, mourning my parents, and fathering a son, I always remembered your past kindness and endured in silence, though my kinsmen and relatives all found it strange. When I was over sixty-five years old, my wife said to me, "You must speak! If you do not speak, I shall kill your son." At that moment, I thought that since I had already passed through a lifetime and was now old and frail, this young son was all I had; therefore, I stopped my wife to prevent her from killing him. That is why I let out this cry." The hermit said, "It is my fault! This was the harassment of a demon." The hero, moved by gratitude but grieved that the task was not accomplished, died in a fit of indignation. Because he escaped the disaster of fire, it is called the Life-Saving Pond; because he died out of gratitude, it is also called the Hero's Pond (烈士池). West of the Hero's Pond is the Three-Beast Stūpa, which is the place where the Tathāgata, while practicing the bodhisattva path, burned his body. At the beginning of the kalpa, in this wilderness, there lived a fox, a rabbit, and a monkey who lived together in harmony despite their different species. At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, wishing to test the one practicing the bodhisattva path, manifested his spirit as an old man and said to the three beasts, "Are you three well and at peace?" "Are you free from fear and alarm?" They replied, "We roam through lush grasses and wander in dense forests; though of different species, we share the same joy, and are both peaceful and happy." The old man said, "I have heard that you two or three are deeply affectionate and close in spirit, and forgetting my own old age and infirmity, I have sought you out from afar. Now, I am truly hungry and weak; what do you have to offer me for food?" They replied, "Please stay here a while; we will personally hasten to seek some." Thereupon, with one heart and humble intent, they went their separate ways to search. The fox went along the riverbank and caught a fresh carp in its mouth, while the ape went among the forest trees and gathered rare flowers and fruits; they both returned to the spot and presented them together to the old man. Only the hare returned empty-handed, leaping about to the left and right. The old man said to them, "In my view, you are not in harmony. The ape and the fox share the same intent and each exerted their minds, yet only the hare returned empty-handed, offering nothing at all. Judging by this, the truth is clear." Having heard this derisive remark, the hare said to the fox and the ape, "Gather plenty of firewood and grass, for I am about to do something." The fox and the ape raced to do so, carrying grass in their mouths and dragging wood; once they had piled it high, the fierce flames were about to blaze. The hare said, "O Benevolent One, my body is lowly and base, and what I sought was difficult to achieve; I venture to offer my humble self to provide this one meal." Having finished speaking, it entered the fire and immediately died. At that time, the old man resumed his form as Śakra (帝釋), cleared away the embers to collect the remains, and after sighing in grief for a long while, said to the fox and the ape, "How could it have come to this! I am moved by its heart and shall not let its traces vanish; I will entrust it to the lunar disk to be passed down to future generations." Therefore, everyone says that the hare in the moon has existed from that time onward. People of later times built a stūpa at this site.

issues: 吾先告汝，汝為魔蔽，不時請留: "I told you before, but you, blinded by Māra, did not ask me in time to stay"; the en makes the being blinded the content of what he told.
en_revised: Three or four *li* to the north of the monastery is a *stūpa*, marking the spot where humans and non-humans followed the World-Honored One and stood still as the Tathāgata was proceeding to the country of Kuśinagara (拘尸那國) to enter *parinirvāṇa*. Not far to the northwest is a *stūpa*, marking the spot where the Buddha last gazed upon the city of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐城). Not far to its south is a vihāra (精舍), with a *stūpa* built in front, marking the site of the Āmrapālī-vana (菴沒羅女園) which she held and offered to the Buddha. Beside the Āmrapālī-vana is a *stūpa*, marking the place where the Tathāgata announced his *nirvāṇa*. Formerly, the Buddha was here and said to Ānanda, "Those who have attained the four bases of psychic power (*catvāraḥ ṛddhi-pādāḥ*) are able to remain for an aeon. The Tathāgata now, how long shall he remain?" In this way he asked three times, but Ānanda did not respond, for he was deluded by the heavenly Māra. Ānanda rose from his seat and went into the forest to meditate in silence. At that time, Māra came to request the Buddha, saying, "The Tathāgata has been in the world teaching and transforming for a long time; those who have been saved from transmigration are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. The joy of extinction—now is the time for it." The World-Honored One placed a small amount of soil on his fingernail and said to Māra, "Is the soil of the earth more, or is the soil on my fingernail more?" He replied, "The soil of the earth is more." The Buddha said, "Those whom I have saved are like the soil on my fingernail, while those who have not been saved are like the soil of the great earth. Three months from now, I shall enter *nirvāṇa*." Hearing this, Māra was joyful and withdrew. Ānanda suddenly had a strange dream while in the woods and came to report it to the Buddha, saying: "While I was in the woods, I dreamed of a great tree with luxuriant branches and leaves and dense shade; a violent wind suddenly arose and scattered it until nothing remained. Could it be that the World-Honored One is about to enter extinction? My heart is filled with fear, so I have come to ask." The Buddha told Ānanda: "I told you before, but you were obscured by Māra and did not request me to remain at the proper time. The Demon King urged me to enter *nirvāṇa* early, and I have already granted him the date; this dream is the sign of that."  Not far from the place where he announced the time of his *nirvāṇa* is a *stūpa* (窣堵波), which is the place where the thousand sons saw their parents. Long ago, there was a *ṛṣi* (仙人) living in seclusion in a rocky valley. In the second month of spring, while he was bathing in a clear stream, a doe followed him to drink and was moved to give birth to a girl. Her appearance was superior to others, but her feet resembled those of a deer. The *ṛṣi* saw her, took her in, and raised her. Later, he ordered her to seek fire. When she reached the hermitage of another *ṛṣi*, lotus flowers appeared in the tracks where her feet stepped. That *ṛṣi* saw this and, deeply amazed, ordered her to walk around his hermitage before she could obtain the fire. The deer-girl followed his instructions, obtained the fire, and returned.  At that time, King Brahmadatta (梵豫王) was hunting and saw the flowers. He followed the tracks to search for their source, was delighted by their strangeness, and took her back with him in his carriage. A physiognomist predicted that she would give birth to a thousand sons. The other wives heard of this and all began to plot against her. When the months and days were full, she gave birth to a single lotus flower. The flower had a thousand petals, and on each petal sat a son. The other wives slandered her, all claiming it was an inauspicious omen, and threw them into the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) river, where they drifted away with the waves. King Ujjayana (烏耆延王) was sightseeing in the lower reaches of the river when he saw a yellow cloud-like canopy floating on the waves; he took it and opened it to find a thousand sons, whom he nursed and raised until they grew up to possess great strength. Relying on his thousand sons, he expanded his territory in all directions, and riding on the momentum of his military victories, he was about to invade this country. At that time, King Brahmadatta (梵豫王) heard of this and was filled with great fear; his military strength was no match for them, and he could think of no solution. At that moment, the Deer Woman (鹿女) knew in her heart that they were her sons, so she said to the King: "Now that the invaders are at our borders and the people are divided, I, your humble servant, in my simple loyalty, can defeat the powerful enemy." The King did not believe her and remained deeply worried and afraid. The Deer Woman then ascended the city tower to await the arrival of the invaders. The thousand sons led their troops and completely surrounded the city, whereupon the Deer Woman called out to them, "Do not commit such a rebellious act! I am your mother, and you are my sons." The thousand sons replied, "What is this absurd talk?" The Deer Woman pressed her two breasts with her hands, and the milk flowed out in a thousand streams; moved by their natural bond, the milk entered each of their mouths. Thereupon, they took off their armor and returned to their lineage, released their weapons and returned to their kin; the two countries rejoiced together, and the common people were at peace. Not far from where the thousand sons returned to their lineage is a stūpa (窣堵波), which marks the old site where the Tathāgata (如來) once walked. He pointed it out to the assembly and said, "In the past, I returned to my lineage here and saw my relatives. If you wish to know who the thousand sons are, they are the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa (賢劫)." To the east of the place where he narrated his former lives, there is an old foundation upon which a stūpa (窣堵波) is built. It occasionally glows with light, and prayers offered there are sometimes granted; these are the remains of the multi-storied lecture hall where the Tathāgata (如來) preached the *Samantamukha-dhāraṇī* (普門陀羅尼) and other sūtras. Not far from the side of the lecture hall is a stūpa containing the relics of half of Ānanda’s body. Not far from here are several hundred stūpas, and though one might wish to determine their exact number, it has never been known; this is the place where a thousand Pratyekabuddhas (獨覺) entered into extinction (寂滅). Within and surrounding the city of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐), there are numerous sacred sites, which are difficult to enumerate in full. The old ruins at these scenic and strategic locations stand as thick as fish scales, but as the years have suddenly changed and the seasons have rapidly shifted, the forests have been destroyed and the ponds have dried up; only decayed stumps and remaining traces are left to be examined in detail.

issues: 更服鮮綺: Mādhava's wife put on fine bright clothes; "his" robes is added (she comes as herself, and the crowd recognises her as his wife).
en_revised: More than thirty *li* to the northwest of the mountain, in a mountain recess, there is a monastery. It rests against a ridge with a lofty foundation, and its pavilions stand upon sparse cliffs. There are more than fifty monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. This is the place where the Bodhisattva Guṇamati (瞿那末底; in the language of the Tang, "Virtue-Wisdom" [德慧]) defeated a non-Buddhist.  Formerly, there was a non-Buddhist in this mountain named Mādhava, who took the Sāṃkhya (僧佉) school as his ancestor and practiced its path. His learning exhausted both internal and external doctrines, his words reached the limits of emptiness and existence, his reputation stood above his contemporaries, and his virtue was esteemed at the time. The king cherished and respected him, calling him the "treasure of the country," and the ministers and commoners revered him, all calling him their "family teacher." Scholars from neighboring countries, hearing of his influence and admiring his virtue, ranked him among the foremost, truly a man of broad attainment. He was supported by the income of two cities, which surrounded his residence as a fief.  At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇamati of South India was quick-witted from his youth; he excelled early in the subtle and profound, his learning mastered the Tripiṭaka, and his reasoning exhausted the Four Noble Truths. Hearing that Mādhava’s theories were extremely profound and subtle, he harbored the intent to blunt his sharp edge. He ordered a disciple to write a letter saying: "I respectfully inquire whether Mādhava is well and at peace. You should forget your weariness and toil, and diligently study your old learning; three years from now, I shall destroy your fine reputation."  In the second and third years, he sent messengers to notify him in this manner. When he was about to set out, he wrote another letter saying: "The time limit has expired; how is your study progressing? I am arriving now; you should be aware of this." Mādhava was filled with great fear and warned his disciples and the inhabitants of his town: "From this day forward, you must not provide lodging to any śramaṇas or followers of heterodox paths; spread this word among yourselves and do not violate this command." At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇamati (德慧) came carrying his staff and arrived at the town of Mādhava. The people kept their agreement, and no one would offer him lodging. The Brahmins further reviled him, saying, "With your shaven head and strange robes, what strange kind of man are you? You should leave quickly; do not stay here!" The Bodhisattva Guṇamati, wishing to defeat the heterodox teachings and hoping to lodge in the town, spoke with a compassionate heart and humble words, saying, "You all practice the pure conduct of worldly truth, while I practice the pure conduct of the ultimate truth; since our pure conduct is the same, why do you reject me?" The Brahmins would not speak to him, but only sought to drive him away. They drove him out of the town and into a great forest. In the forest, packs of fierce beasts acted with violence. A man of pure faith, fearing he might be harmed by the beasts, bound together a torch and took up a staff, saying to the Bodhisattva, "There is a Bodhisattva Guṇamati of South India whose reputation has spread far and wide, and who intends to come here for a debate; therefore, the lord of this town, fearing the loss of his good name, has strictly decreed that no śramaṇa be allowed to stay. Fearing you might be harmed by the creatures, I have come to assist you. Go now and be at peace; have no other worries." Guṇamati said, "I must tell you, pure believer, that I am Guṇamati." Having heard this, the pure believer showed even deeper respect and said to Guṇamati, "Since it is as you say, you should depart quickly." He then left the deep forest and rested in an empty marsh. The pure believer lit a fire and held his bow, patrolling around him; when the night had ended, he said to Guṇamati, "You may go now, for I fear people may hear of this and come to harm you." Guṇamati thanked him, saying, "I shall not forget your kindness." Thereupon he departed. Arriving at the royal palace, he said to the gatekeeper, "There is a śramaṇa who has come from afar; he requests the king's gracious permission to debate with Mādhava (摩沓婆)." Hearing this, the king was surprised and said, "This is a delusional man." He immediately ordered an envoy to go to Mādhava’s residence to proclaim the royal decree, saying, "An extraordinary śramaṇa has come seeking a debate; the debate hall has now been cleansed and prepared, and an announcement has been sent out far and near; we await your arrival and hope you will grace us with your presence." Mādhava asked the king's envoy, "Is it not the Śāstra Master Guṇamati (德慧) of South India?" The envoy replied, "It is." Upon hearing this, Mādhava was very displeased, but as the matter was difficult to decline, he proceeded to the debate hall. The king, ministers, scholars, commoners, and noble families all gathered to listen to the profound discourse. Guṇamati first established his thesis, and by the time the sun had set, Mādhava excused himself on the grounds of his advanced age and the dullness of his wit in responding quickly, requesting to return home to reflect so that he might respond to the challenge later. Every point was met with a request to return home, and when he ascended the seat the next morning, he ultimately offered no counter-arguments. On the sixth day, he vomited blood and died. As he was about to expire, he looked at his wife and commanded, "You possess great talent; do not forget this shame!" After Mādhava died, his death was concealed and not announced; his wife changed into fine, colorful robes and came to the debate hall. The crowd broke into a hubbub, saying to one another, "Mādhava is conceited about his own talent and is ashamed to face Guṇamati, so he has sent his wife instead; the difference in their caliber is now clear." Guṇamati Bodhisattva (德慧菩薩) said to his wife, "The one who could control you, I have already subdued." Mādhava’s wife, realizing the difficulty, withdrew. The King asked, "What was that secret conversation, that she became silent?" Guṇamati replied, "Alas, Mādhava is dead! His wife intended to come and debate with me." The King asked, "How did you know this? I wish you would explain it to me." Guṇamati said, "When his wife came, her face bore the look of mourning and her voice was filled with grief and resentment; therefore, I knew that Mādhava was dead. 'The one who could control you' referred to her husband." The King ordered an envoy to go and observe, and it was indeed as discussed. The King then apologized, saying, "The Buddha-Dharma is profound and mysterious; brilliant sages follow in succession. By practicing the Way through non-action, all sentient beings are moistened by its transformation. According to the ancient laws of the state, there is a constant practice of praising virtue." Guṇamati said, "Though I am ignorant, I embody the Way and dwell in purity. If one maintains integrity and seeks to benefit others, then to promote and guide them, one must first crush their arrogance. As for using expedient means to gather and transform them, now is the time. I only wish that Your Majesty would assign the descendants of the households in Mādhava’s fief to serve the monastery (saṃghārāma) for a thousand generations, so as to leave a warning for future ages and spread this beauty boundlessly. And may that man of pure faith who protected me have his blessings extended to his descendants, and may his food and provisions be the same as the monks', so as to encourage the pure-hearted and praise profound virtue." Thereupon, this monastery was built to commemorate this remarkable event. Initially, after Mādhava was defeated in debate, some ten or more Brahmins fled to a neighboring country to escape the disgrace. They reported the humiliation to various heretics (tīrthikas) and recruited talented individuals to come and wash away their previous shame. Since the king esteemed and respected Guṇamati (德慧), he went in person to request him, saying: "Now these heretics, overestimating their own strength, have formed a clique and dared to sound the drum of debate; I only wish that the Great Master would crush these heterodox sects." Guṇamati said: "It is appropriate to assemble the debaters." Thereupon, the heretical scholars comforted one another with joy, saying: "Today, we are certain to be victorious over him." When the heretics began to expound their doctrines, Guṇamati Bodhisattva said: "These heretics fled the disgrace and went far away; according to the king's prior decree, they are all outcasts, so how can I engage in a debate with them?" Guṇamati had a seat-carrier (a servant who carried his portable seat) who had long listened to his debates and was quite familiar with the subtle meanings; he stood by his side, listening to their lofty discourse. Guṇamati patted his seat and said: "Seat, you may debate with them." The assembly was entirely shocked and found his command strange. At that time, the seat-carrier immediately launched his challenge; profound meanings gushed forth like a spring, and his clear eloquence responded to every point. After three rounds, the heretics lost their tenets; their sharpness was severely blunted, and their wings were broken. Ever since they were defeated in debate, they were established as the households of the monastery (saṃghārāma).

issues: 非汝所祈，非我能遂 means wishes are fulfilled neither by your praying nor by my power (only merit fulfils them), not "what you pray for is not something I can grant"; 如來於此納故衣 is where he mended (patched) old clothes, not "put on an old garment".
en_revised: To the east of the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) is a vihāra (精舍), one hundred and sixty or seventy feet high, with a base more than twenty paces wide, built of blue bricks and plastered with lime. The tiered niches all contain golden images, and the four walls are carved with exquisite designs, some in the form of linked pearls, others as celestial beings. At the top is placed a golden-copper āmalaka fruit (also called a treasure vase, or a treasure terrace). The eastern side is connected to a multi-storied pavilion with eaves and roofs rising in three distinct tiers; the rafters, pillars, beams, doors, and windows are decorated with gold and silver carvings and inlaid with pearls and jade. The inner chambers and deep halls have three sets of connecting doors. On the left and right of the outer gate are niche chambers; on the left is an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva (觀自在菩薩), and on the right is an image of Maitreya Bodhisattva (慈氏菩薩), both cast in white silver and over ten feet high. On the original site of the vihāra, King Aśoka (無憂王) first built a small vihāra, which was later expanded by a Brahmin. Initially, there was a Brahmin who did not believe in the Buddha’s teachings and worshipped Maheśvara (大自在天). Hearing that the deity resided in the Snow Mountains, he went there with his younger brother to seek the fulfillment of his vows. The deity said, "All wishes and prayers are fulfilled only when one has merit. It is not your praying that fulfils them, nor my power." The Brahmin asked, "What merit should I cultivate to fulfill my heart's desire?" The deity replied, "If you wish to plant good seeds and seek a superior field of merit, the Mahā-bodhi is the place where the Buddha attained the fruit of enlightenment. You should return quickly, go to the Mahā-bodhi, build a great vihāra, dig a large water pond, and perform various offerings; then your wishes shall be fulfilled." The Brahmin, having received the divine command, conceived great faith and returned together; the elder brother built a vihāra (精舍) and the younger brother excavated a water pond. Thereupon, they performed grand offerings and diligently sought the fulfillment of their heart’s desires, which were eventually realized as they became high ministers to the king, and all the emoluments and rewards they received were given away as alms. Once the vihāra was completed, they sought to recruit craftsmen to fashion an image of the Tathāgata as he first attained Buddhahood. A long time passed, and no one responded to the call. After a while, a Brahmin came and told the assembly, "I am skilled at depicting the wondrous form of the Tathāgata." The assembly asked, "Now that we are to create the image, what do you require?" He replied, "Only scented clay. It should be placed inside the vihāra, along with a single lamp for illumination. Once I have entered, seal the door firmly; it may only be opened after six months." The monastic assembly followed his instructions. With four days still remaining before the six months were up, the assembly became alarmed and curious, and they opened the door to look inside. They saw the Buddha image inside the vihāra looking majestic, sitting cross-legged with the right foot on top, the left hand withdrawn, and the right hand hanging down, facing east and appearing as solemn as if it were alive. The pedestal was four feet two inches high and twelve feet five inches wide; the image was eleven feet five inches tall, with a distance of eight feet eight inches between the knees and six feet two inches between the shoulders. Its auspicious marks were complete and its compassionate face seemed real, except that the polishing above the right breast was not yet finished. Since the man was nowhere to be seen, they realized it was a divine manifestation, and the assembly sighed with sorrow and earnestly prayed to understand. There was a śramaṇa of simple and honest character who had a dream in which the former brahmin appeared and said to him, "I am Maitreya Bodhisattva (慈氏菩薩); fearing that the thoughts of craftsmen could not fathom the holy countenance, I came in person to depict the Buddha's image. As for the lowered right hand, formerly when the Tathāgata was about to realize the fruit of Buddhahood, the celestial Māra came to harass him, and an earth deity announced his arrival. One of them emerged first to help the Buddha subjugate the demon, but the Tathāgata told him, 'Do not be worried or afraid; I shall surely subjugate him through the power of forbearance.' The demon king asked, 'Who will be the clear witness?' The Tathāgata then lowered his hand and pointed to the ground, saying, 'This is the witness.' At that time, the second earth deity emerged to bear witness; therefore, the hand of the present image imitates that former posture of lowering." The assembly, knowing of this spiritual manifestation, was filled with sorrow and reverence. Consequently, where the area above the breast was not yet finished, they filled it with various precious substances, and adorned it with pearl necklaces, jeweled crowns, and rare treasures.  After King Śaśāṅka (設賞迦王) had felled the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree, he wished to destroy this image; however, once he beheld its compassionate countenance, his heart could not bear it, and as he turned his carriage to return, he commanded a high minister, saying, "You should remove this Buddha image and install a figure of Maheśvara (大自在天)." Having received the decree, the minister was afraid and sighed, saying, "If I destroy the Buddha image, I shall incur calamity for kalpas to come; yet if I disobey the King's command, I shall lose my life and have my clan exterminated. In such a dilemma, what is the proper course of action!" He then summoned men of faith to serve as laborers and built a brick wall across the front of the image; feeling ashamed that it would be in total darkness, he also placed a bright lamp inside, and on the front of the brick wall, he painted a picture of Maheśvara. When the work was completed, he reported back to the King. Upon hearing this, the King was terrified; his entire body broke out in pustules, his skin and flesh cracked and split, and before long, he died. The minister hurried back and destroyed the wall that had served as a barrier. Although many days had passed, the lamp was still not extinguished. The image remains to this day, and the divine craftsmanship is unimpaired. Since it is situated in a secluded chamber where lamps are kept burning in succession, one who wishes to behold the compassionate countenance cannot examine it clearly; one must hold a large, bright mirror in the morning to reflect light inside, and only then can the sacred image be seen. Those who see it naturally feel an increase in sorrow and reverence.  The Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment on the eighth day of the second half of the Indian month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the eighth day of the third month in our calendar. According to the Sthavira school, however, he attained perfect enlightenment on the fifteenth day of the second half of the month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the third month. At that time, the Tathāgata was thirty years old; others say he was thirty-five.  To the north of the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) is the place where the Buddha walked in meditation. After the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment, he did not rise from his seat for seven days, remaining in silent meditation. When he arose, he went to the north of the Mahā-bodhi and walked in meditation for seven days, pacing back and forth from east to west for more than ten paces. Extraordinary flowers appeared in his footprints, numbering eighteen in total. Later generations built a brick foundation here, more than three feet high. I have heard from ancient records that this sacred foundation indicates the length of a person's life: if one first makes a sincere vow and then measures it, the number will increase or decrease according to the length of one's lifespan. To the north of the meditation foundation, on the right side of the path, upon a large rock, there is a great shrine (精舍) containing a Buddha image that is looking upward with its eyes raised. In the past, the Tathāgata spent seven days here gazing at the Mahā-bodhi tree (菩提樹) without once averting his eyes. He did this to repay the tree for its kindness, and thus he kept it in his view. Not far to the west of the Mahā-bodhi tree, in a great shrine (精舍), there is a brass Buddha image adorned with rare jewels, standing and facing east. In front of it is a blue stone with wonderful patterns and extraordinary colors; this is where, when the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment, the Brahma King (Brahmā) built a hall of seven treasures and Lord Indra (Śakra) constructed a throne of seven treasures, upon which the Buddha meditated for seven days, emitting a wondrous light that illuminated the Mahā-bodhi tree. As the time since the Sage’s passing is long, the treasures have turned into stone.  Not far to the south of the Mahā-bodhi tree, there is a stūpa over a hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). When the Bodhisattva had bathed in the Nairañjanā River and was about to proceed to the Mahā-bodhi tree, he secretly pondered what he should use for a seat. He soon realized that he required clean grass. Lord Indra (天帝釋) transformed himself into a grass-cutter, carrying grass and following the path. The Bodhisattva said to him, "Could you bestow upon me some of the grass you are carrying?" The transformed being, hearing this request, respectfully offered the grass, which the Bodhisattva accepted, holding it as he proceeded forward.  Not far to the northeast of where he received the grass, there is a stūpa, which marks the place where bluebirds and herds of deer presented auspicious omens when the Bodhisattva was about to attain the fruit of Buddhahood. In India, such signs are considered favorable omens; therefore, the gods of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsa-deva) conformed to the ways of the world, and the flocks followed, flying and circling to manifest their spiritual power and reveal the holiness of the site. To the east of the Mahā-bodhi tree, on either side of the main road, there is a stūpa; these are the places where the King of Māras disturbed the Bodhisattva. When the Bodhisattva was about to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, the King of Māras urged him to accept the position of a Wheel-Turning King; when his entreaties failed, he returned in deep sorrow. The daughters of the King of Māras requested to go and seduce him, but through the Bodhisattva’s divine power, their beautiful appearances withered and changed; they withdrew supporting one another, frail and leaning on staves. To the northwest of the Mahā-bodhi tree (菩提樹), inside a shrine (精舍), there is an image of Kāśyapa Buddha; it is renowned for its spiritual efficacy and frequently emits a brilliant light. According to ancient records, if a person with utmost sincerity circumambulates it seven times, they will attain the knowledge of past lives in whatever place they are reborn. To the northwest of the Kāśyapa Buddha shrine are two brick chambers, each containing an image of an earth deity. In the past, when the Tathāgata was about to attain perfect enlightenment, one reported the arrival of Māra, and the other served as a witness for the Buddha. Later generations, mindful of their service, depicted their forms to honor their virtue. Not far to the west of the Mahā-bodhi tree enclosure, there is a stūpa called the Saffron (郁金香) Stūpa, over forty feet high, which was built by a merchant lord of the country of Jāguḍa (漕炬吒國). Formerly, in the country of Jāguḍa, there was a great merchant lord who worshiped heavenly deities and offered sacrifices to seek blessings, while holding the Buddha’s teachings in contempt and disbelieving in cause and effect. Later, he led a group of merchants to trade goods, sailing on the southern sea, when they encountered a storm and lost their way. Drifting on the waves for three years, their provisions were exhausted and they could not even secure enough food to survive. The people on the ship, unable to plan for the next day, joined their efforts and shared their resolve, calling upon the deities they served; yet, though their minds were weary with anxiety, their secret prayers were not answered. Suddenly, they saw a great mountain with towering cliffs and steep ridges, where two suns shone together, casting a brilliant, double light. At that time, the merchants comforted one another, saying, "We are fortunate; having passed this great mountain, we should stop here and find peace and happiness." The merchant leader said, "It is not a mountain, but a makara-fish. The towering cliffs and steep ridges are its whiskers and mane, and the two suns shining together are the light of its eyes." Before his voice had faded, the ship drifted toward it. Thereupon, the merchant leader told his companions, "I have heard that the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara can bestow peace and happiness in the midst of all dangers and difficulties; we should each, with utmost sincerity, call upon his name." They immediately joined their voices in unison, taking refuge and reciting his name. The towering mountain then vanished, and the two suns also disappeared. Suddenly, they saw a śramaṇa, dignified and composed, holding a staff and walking through the void, who came to rescue them from drowning; before long, they arrived at their own country.  Because of this, their faith became firm and steadfast, and they sought merit without wavering. They built a stūpa and performed offerings, coating it from top to bottom with saffron-scented mud. Having developed this faith, they led their companions to personally pay homage to the sacred sites and view the Mahā-bodhi tree. Before they had time to return home, a month had already passed. As the merchants traveled together, they said to one another, "The mountains and rivers are vast and our homeland is far away; since we are here, who is there to sweep and clean the stūpa we previously built?" Having said this, they circled around to this spot and suddenly saw the stūpa. Astonished at how this could be, they went forward to examine it and found it was the very stūpa built by their own country. Therefore, in India today, it is known by the name of Saffron. At the southeast corner of the wall surrounding the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹), beside a banyan tree (nyagrodha), there is a vihāra (精舍) next to a stūpa, containing a statue of the Buddha in a seated posture. In the past, when the Tathāgata first attained the fruit of Buddhahood, the Great Brahmā King (Mahābrahmā-devarāja) here entreated him to turn the wheel of the wonderful Dharma. Within the enclosure of the Mahā-bodhi, there are large stūpas at each of the four corners. In the past, after the Tathāgata had received the auspicious grass (kuśa), he proceeded toward the Mahā-bodhi; he first passed by the four corners, and the great earth shook, only becoming still when he reached the Vajrāsana (金剛座). Within the enclosure of the tree, sacred sites are arranged like the scales of a fish, and it is difficult to enumerate them all.  Outside the enclosure of the Mahā-bodhi, to the southwest, there is a stūpa marking the former residence of the two milkmaids who offered the milk gruel. Beside it is a stūpa where the milkmaids boiled the gruel. Next to this stūpa is the place where the Tathāgata received the gruel. Outside the south gate of the Mahā-bodhi enclosure is a large pond, over seven hundred paces in circumference, with clear, mirror-like waves where dragons and fish dwell; it was excavated by two Brahmin brothers acting under the command of Maheśvara (大自在天). To the south of this is another pond; in the past, when the Tathāgata had first attained perfect enlightenment and wished to bathe, Śakra-devānām-indra (天帝釋) manifested this pond for the Buddha. To the west is a large stone; after the Buddha had washed his robes and wished to dry them, Śakra-devānām-indra brought it from the Great Snow Mountains (Himālaya). Beside it is a stūpa where the Tathāgata mended his old robes. Further to the south, in the forest, is a stūpa marking the place where the Tathāgata accepted the offering of an old garment from a poor elderly woman.
li_quote: Beside the rock is a stupa where the Tathāgata mended his old clothes.

issues: 入兩安居 / 解兩安居: 兩 here stands for 雨 (the rains retreat, varṣā); "two-part rains retreat" is invented.
en_revised: Outside the north gate of the Bodhi tree is the Mahābodhi Monastery (摩訶菩提僧伽藍), which was built by a former king of the country of Siṃhala (僧伽羅國). It has six courtyards and three-storied pavilions, surrounded by walls thirty to forty feet high; the workmanship is of the utmost ingenuity, and the painted decorations are exquisite. As for the Buddha images, they are cast in gold and silver, and all their adornments are inlaid with precious gems. The various stupas are lofty, spacious, and exquisitely decorated, containing the relics of the Tathāgata; the bone relics are as large as a finger joint, lustrous, pure white, and translucent inside and out. The flesh relics are like large pearls, with a color tinged with reddish-blue. Every year, on the full moon day of the month of the Tathāgata’s great spiritual manifestations, they are displayed to the public (This is the thirtieth day of the twelfth month in India, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the first month here). At this time, they sometimes emit light or rain down flowers. The community of monks numbers nearly one thousand; they study the teachings of the Mahāyāna and the Sthavira school, their monastic discipline is pure and strict, and their conduct is upright and bright. Formerly, in the southern sea, there was the country of Siṃhala, whose king was purely devoted to the Buddha-dharma, a faith arising from his own nature. He had a younger cousin who became a monk and, longing to see the sacred sites of the Buddha, traveled far to India. He stayed in various monasteries, but all of them treated him with contempt as a border-dweller. He then returned to his own country, and the king personally went out to welcome him. The śramaṇa was sorrowful and distressed, as if he were unable to speak. The king said, "What burden do you carry that causes such deep melancholy?" The śramaṇa said, "Relying on the prestige of the state, I traveled to distant lands to inquire after the Way. Living as a stranger in foreign territories, I endured the cold and the heat, and at every turn I encountered humiliation and was mocked for my speech. Bearing such sorrow and shame, how could I be happy?" The king asked, "What do you mean by this?" He replied, "I sincerely wish that Your Majesty would take the field of merit to heart and establish a monastery (saṃghārāma) in India. This would both honor the holy sites and bring you great fame, while the resulting merit would support the late king and its blessings would reach your descendants." The king said, "This is a wonderful idea; why did I not hear of it sooner?" He then sent the treasures of his country as an offering to the King of India.  Having accepted the tribute and wishing to show kindness to those from afar, the King of India said to the envoy, "What should I now give as a return gift for your mission?" The envoy said, "The King of Siṃhala (僧伽羅) bows his head to the Great Auspicious King of India! Your majesty’s prestige and virtue extend far, and your benevolent grace reaches to distant places. The śramaṇas of our lowly land, admiring your influence and transformation, dared to travel to your superior kingdom to pay their respects at the holy sites. Yet, when they stayed in the monasteries, they were not provided with lodging; they suffered extreme hardship and returned home having endured shame. I humbly propose a far-reaching plan to set an example for future generations: to build this monastery in India so that traveling mendicants may have a place to rest, the two countries may enjoy friendly relations, and travelers may pass between them without end." The king said, "The Tathāgata’s subtle influence has passed, but his legacy remains; you may choose any one of the holy sites." The envoy accepted the command and returned to report the mission. The ministers offered their congratulations, and the king then gathered the śramaṇas to deliberate on the construction. The śramaṇas said, "The Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) is the place where all Buddhas of the past and future attain holiness; having examined the various opinions, there is no better plan than this." Thereupon, the king gave up the treasures of his country and built this monastery, assigning monks from his own country to perform the offerings, and he engraved a copper plate as a record, which stated: "To provide for all without partiality is the supreme teaching of the Buddhas; to aid those with affinity through wisdom is the clear instruction of the ancient sages. Now I, this humble person, having inherited the great royal undertaking, have built this monastery to commemorate the holy site, so that the resulting merit may benefit my ancestors and its grace may extend to the common people. Only monks from my own country shall have authority here, and any of my countrymen shall be treated the same as the monks. May this be passed down to descendants, forever and ever without end." For this reason, this monastery is mostly occupied by monks from the country of Siṃhala (師子國).  More than ten li south of the Mahā-bodhi, holy sites are adjacent to one another, and it is difficult to list them all. Every year, when the bhikṣus conclude the rains retreat (vārṣika), clergy and laity from the four directions, numbering hundreds of thousands,, for seven days and seven nights, carry incense and flowers, play music, and travel throughout the forest to pay homage and make offerings. According to the holy teachings of the Buddha, the monks of India all enter the rains retreat on the first day of the first half of the month of Śrāvaṇa, which corresponds to the sixteenth day of the fifth month here; they conclude the rains retreat on the fifteenth day of the second half of the month of Aśvayuja, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the eighth month here. The names of the Indian months are based on the stars and have remained unchanged from ancient times to the present; among all the schools, there is no discrepancy. It is because the local dialects were not fully reconciled and there were errors in translation regarding the division of time and the calculation of months that these discrepancies have arisen; therefore, the retreat is entered on the sixteenth day of the fourth month and concluded on the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
